subject: Pediatrics
topic: Ileocolic Intussusception Non-Operative Reduction vs Emergency Laparotomy
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Intussusception management: Most common cause of intestinal obstruction in children 6 to 36 months (idiopathic, hypertrophy of Peyer patches following viral infection). Clinical triad (present in < 50%): Episodic colicky severe abdominal pain (legs drawn to chest), vomiting, and "CURRANT JELLY" STOOLS (blood and mucus from bowel ischemia). Examination: Sausage-shaped mass in right upper quadrant, empty right lower quadrant (Dance sign). DIAGNOSTIC TEST OF CHOICE: ABDOMINAL ULTRASOUND (demonstrates "TARGET SIGN" / "DONUT SIGN" on transverse view, and "pseudokidney sign" on longitudinal view). FIRST-LINE MANAGEMENT: If NO PERITONITIS AND NO PERFORATION: AIR OR WATER-SOLUBLE CONTRAST ENEMA under fluoroscopic or ultrasound guidance (both diagnostic and therapeutic; success rate > 80-90%). CONTRAINDICATIONS TO ENEMA: PERITONITIS, PNEUMOPERITONEUM (free air on X-ray indicating perforation), or hypovolemic shock. If peritonitis or perforation is present -> IMMEDIATE EMERGENCE EXPLORATORY LAPAROTOMY, NOT ENEMA!
necessaryInference: Identify ileocolic intussusception by clinical ultrasound target sign, and deduce that stable patients without peritonitis require non-operative pneumatic (air) enema reduction, while signs of perforation mandate emergency surgical exploration.
strongestDistractor: Immediate emergent exploratory laparotomy with primary bowel resection and ileostomy creation
distractorExclusion: Emergency laparotomy is indicated only if signs of peritonitis, hemodynamic instability, or radiographic bowel perforation are present; stable patients are managed with pneumatic or hydrostatic enema reduction.

references.label: Marsicovetere P, Ivatury SJ, White B, Holubar SD. Intestinal Intussusception: Etiology, Diagnosis, and Management. Clin Colon Rectal Surg. 2017;30(1):30-39. PMID: 28144210.

subject: Pediatrics
topic: Midgut Volvulus with Malrotation Diagnosis and Urgent Ladd Procedure
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Malrotation and Midgut Volvulus: Embryology: Failure of normal 270-degree counterclockwise rotation of midgut around superior mesenteric artery (SMA) during week 10. Result: Cecum is in right upper quadrant; duodenum does not cross midline; gut is suspended by a narrow mesenteric stalk; fibrous PERITONEAL BANDS OF LADD cross and compress duodenum. VOLVULUS: The narrow mesenteric pedicle twists around the SMA, causing acute duodenal obstruction and TOTAL MIDGUT ISCHEMIA/INFARCTION. Clinical presentation: SUDDEN-ONSET BILIOUS EMESIS IN A NEONATE OR INFANT (< 1 month of age). BILIOUS EMESIS IN A NEONATE IS A SURGICAL EMERGENCY! DIAGNOSTIC GOLD STANDARD: UPPER GASTROINTESTINAL (UGI) FLUOROSCOPY SERIES: Demonstrates duodenal C-loop failing to cross the vertebral midline, ligament of Treitz displaced to the right of the spine, and a "CORKSCREW" or "BIRD-BEAK" appearance of the twisted distal duodenum. Treatment: EMERGENT SURGERY (LADD PROCEDURE: untwisting volvulus counterclockwise, dividing Ladd bands, widening mesenteric base, placing small bowel on right and colon on left, and appendectomy).
necessaryInference: Synthesize that sudden bilious vomiting in an infant represents midgut volvulus until proven otherwise, diagnosed by upper GI series demonstrating abnormal ligament of Treitz positioning, and treated with emergent Ladd procedure to prevent total intestinal necrosis.
strongestDistractor: Immediate pneumatic contrast enema under fluoroscopy to achieve hydrostatic reduction of the volvulus
distractorExclusion: Contrast enemas treat intussusception; midgut volvulus is a twisting of the midgut around the SMA and requires emergent surgical untwisting (Ladd procedure), not an enema.

references.label: Millar AJ, Rode H, Cywes S. Malrotation and volvulus in infancy and childhood. Semin Pediatr Surg. 2003;12(4):229-236. PMID: 14655161.

subject: Pediatrics
topic: Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia Immediate Resuscitation and Management
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia (CDH): Embryology: Failure of pleuroperitoneal membranes to fuse with septum transversum and esophageal mesentery during week 8-10. > 85% occur on the LEFT POSTEROLATERAL side (BOCHDALEK HERNIA; right-sided is Morgagni). Consequences: Herniation of abdominal viscera (stomach, bowel loops, spleen) into thoracic cavity causes SEVERE PULMONARY HYPOPLASIA AND PERSISTENT PULMONARY HYPERTENSION (PPHN). Clinical presentation: Neonate with severe respiratory distress, scaphoid abdomen, barrel chest, shifted heart sounds (to the right), and absent breath sounds on the left with bowel sounds in the hemithorax. IMMEDIATE DELIVERY ROOM RESUSCITATION RULES: 1. IMMEDIATE ENDOTRACHEAL INTUBATION! 2. BAG-VALVE-MASK (BVM) VENTILATION IS STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED! BVM forces air into the stomach and herniated bowel loops, causing massive gastrointestinal distension that further compresses the hypoplastic lungs and mediastinum, precipitating immediate fatal cardiovascular collapse. 3. Place a continuous-suction nasogastric or orogastric tube to decompress stomach. SURGICAL TIMING: CDH IS NO LONGER A SURGICAL EMERGENCY! Early surgery worsens survival. SURGERY IS DELAYED (often 48-72 hours) until pulmonary hypertension and hemodynamic stability are achieved (pre-ductal SpO2 > 85%, normal echocardiogram).
necessaryInference: Deduce that delivery room resuscitation of congenital diaphragmatic hernia strictly mandates immediate endotracheal intubation while avoiding bag-valve-mask ventilation, and that definitive surgical repair is delayed until pulmonary hypertension is stabilized.
strongestDistractor: Vigorous bag-valve-mask ventilation with 100% oxygen followed by immediate emergent exploratory laparotomy within 2 hours of delivery
distractorExclusion: Bag-valve-mask ventilation is strictly contraindicated because it aerates the intrathoracic bowel and crushes the hypoplastic lungs; surgery must be delayed until pulmonary hypertension is medically stabilized.

references.label: Hedrick HL. Management of Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia. Clin Perinatol. 2022;49(4):871-884. PMID: 36328608.

subject: Pediatrics
topic: Necrotizing Enterocolitis Pneumatosis Intestinalis and Indications for Laparotomy
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Necrotizing Enterocolitis (NEC): Most common gastrointestinal medical-surgical emergency in PREMATURE / VERY LOW BIRTH WEIGHT (< 1500 g) infants. Pathophysiology: Immature gut mucosal barrier + enteral formula feeding + bacterial colonization -> mucosal breakdown, bacterial invasion, transmural ischemic necrosis. RISK FACTORS: Prematurity, low birth weight, FORMULA FEEDING (breast milk is protective!), hypoxic-ischemic events, congenital heart disease. Clinical signs: Abdominal distension, feeding intolerance / gastric residuals, bilious vomiting, bloody stools (hematochezia), lethargy, temperature instability, apnea. DIAGNOSTIC HALLMARK ON ABDOMINAL X-RAY: 1. PNEUMATOSIS INTESTINALIS (gas in bowel wall; linear or curvilinear radiolucencies parallel to bowel lumen; PATHOGNOMONIC!). 2. Portal venous gas (branching radiolucency over liver). MEDICAL MANAGEMENT: Bowel rest (NPO), nasogastric decompression, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (ampicillin + gentamicin + metronidazole), TPN, serial abdominal X-rays every 6 hours. DEFINITIVE INDICATION FOR EMERGENCY SURGERY (LAPAROTOMY / PERITONEAL DRAIN): PNEUMOPERITONEUM (free intraperitoneal air on X-ray, seen as "Football sign" on supine X-ray or air under diaphragm on cross-table lateral/left lateral decubitus view), indicating BOWEL PERFORATION.
necessaryInference: Identify necrotizing enterocolitis by radiographic pneumatosis intestinalis in a premature formula-fed infant, and deduce that medical management is indicated initially, while pneumoperitoneum (free air) represents an absolute indication for emergency surgical laparotomy.
strongestDistractor: Immediate emergent exploratory laparotomy upon initial discovery of linear pneumatosis intestinalis
distractorExclusion: Pneumatosis intestinalis without perforation is managed medically with bowel rest, antibiotics, and serial imaging; emergency surgery is indicated only when pneumoperitoneum (free air) confirms bowel perforation or medical therapy fails.

references.label: Neu J, Walker WA. Necrotizing enterocolitis. N Engl J Med. 2011;364(3):255-264. PMID: 21247316.

subject: Pediatrics
topic: Hirschsprung Disease Rectal Suction Biopsy Gold Standard Diagnosis
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Hirschsprung Disease (Congenital Aganglionic Megacolon): Embryology: Failure of CRANIAL NEURAL CREST CELLS to migrate craniocaudally into distal bowel wall during weeks 5 to 12. Result: ABSENCE OF PARASYMPATHETIC GANGLION CELLS in both SUBMUCOSAL (MEISSNER) and MYENTERIC (AUERBACH) PLEXUSES. The aganglionic segment remains PERMANENTLY CONTRACTED / SPASM, causing functional distal intestinal obstruction and massive proximal dilation ("megacolon"). ASSOCIATIONS: Down syndrome (Trisomy 21), RET proto-oncogene inactivating mutations. Clinical presentation: FAILURE TO PASS MECONIUM WITHIN 48 HOURS OF BIRTH in a full-term infant, abdominal distension, bilious emesis. Digital rectal exam: Tight anal sphincter; withdrawal of examining finger produces an EXPLOSIVE EXPULSION OF FLATUS AND LIQUID STOOL ("squirt sign" or "blast sign"). Initial imaging: CONTRAST ENEMA: Demonstrates a narrow, spastic aganglionic rectosigmoid segment with a proximal CONE-SHAPED "TRANSITION ZONE" leading into a massively dilated proximal colon. GOLD STANDARD DEFINITIVE DIAGNOSIS: RECTAL SUCTION BIOPSY (mucosa and submucosa obtained 2-3 cm above dentate line; reveals ABSENCE OF GANGLION CELLS and hypertrophic nerve trunks staining positive for acetylcholinesterase).
necessaryInference: Identify Hirschsprung disease by failure to pass meconium within 48 hours, squirt sign on rectal exam, and transition zone on contrast enema, and deduce that rectal suction biopsy demonstrating absent ganglion cells is the gold standard diagnostic test.
strongestDistractor: Full-thickness surgical laparotomy biopsy of the dilated ascending colon demonstrating absence of mucosal ganglion cells
distractorExclusion: Biopsy must be taken from the narrowed, aganglionic distal rectum (not the normally innervated dilated proximal colon), and can be performed non-operatively at the bedside via rectal suction biopsy.

references.label: Langer JC. Hirschsprung disease. Curr Opin Pediatr. 2013;25(3):368-374. PMID: 23615174.

subject: Pediatrics
topic: Biliary Atresia Direct Hyperbilirubinemia and Urgent Kasai Hepatoportoenterostomy
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Biliary Atresia: Progressive fibro-obliterative destruction of extrahepatic biliary tree. Most common cause of pediatric liver transplantation. CLINICAL PRESENTATION: Infant appears normal at birth, then develops PROGRESSIVE JAUNDICE AT 2 TO 8 WEEKS OF AGE. Crucial findings: 1. DIRECT (CONJUGATED) HYPERBILIRUBINEMIA (Direct bilirubin > 20% of total bilirubin, or > 1.0 mg/dL; ALWAYS PATHOLOGICAL!). 2. ACHOLIC (CLAY-COLORED / WHITE) STOOLS (lack of bile pigment stercobilin in gut). 3. DARK, TEA-COLORED URINE (conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and excreted in urine). 4. Hepatomegaly. INITIAL TEST: ABDOMINAL ULTRASOUND (rules out choledochal cyst; reveals absent or fibrotic gallbladder and "TRIANGULAR CORD SIGN" = fibrous ductal remnant anterior to portal vein). Confirmatory: HIDA cholescintigraphy (uptake by liver but ZERO EXCRETION into small bowel even at 24 hours). GOLD STANDARD: Intraoperative cholangiogram. TREATMENT: URGENT KASAI HEPATOPORTOENTEROSTOMY (Roux-en-Y anastomosing jejunum to porta hepatis). SURGICAL TIMING IS CRITICAL: MUST BE PERFORMED BEFORE 60 DAYS OF LIFE (< 2 months) to prevent irreversible biliary cirrhosis!
necessaryInference: Synthesize that conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with acholic stools at 4 weeks of age represents biliary atresia, requiring prompt evaluation and urgent Kasai hepatoportoenterostomy before 60 days of age to prevent irreversible cirrhosis.
strongestDistractor: Immediate initiation of intensive phototherapy and phenobarbital with scheduled elective re-evaluation at 6 months of age
distractorExclusion: Phototherapy is used for unconjugated (indirect) hyperbilirubinemia; conjugated hyperbilirubinemia is not treated with phototherapy (causes bronze baby syndrome) and delaying surgery beyond 60 days leads to irreversible cirrhosis.

references.label: Hartley JL, Davenport M, Kelly DA. Biliary atresia. Lancet. 2009;374(9702):1704-1713. PMID: 19837255.

subject: Pediatrics
topic: Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis Metabolic Resuscitation Before Surgery
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Infantile Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis (IHPS): Hypertrophy and hyperplasia of the circular muscle layer of the pylorus. Epidemiology: Firstborn males (4:1 male predominance), age 3 to 6 weeks, associated with macrolide exposure (erythromycin/azithromycin). Presentation: NON-BILIOUS, PROJECTILE POSTPRANDIAL EMESIS (infant is immediately "hungry" and eager to feed again: "hungry vomiter"). Exam: Firm, mobile, 1-2 cm "OLIVE-SHAPED" MASS in right upper quadrant / epigastrium; visible peristaltic waves. DIAGNOSTIC ULTRASOUND: Pyloric muscle thickness >= 3-4 mm and channel length >= 14 mm. METABOLIC DERANGEMENT: Gastric vomiting causes loss of HCl and water -> HYPOCHLOREMIC, HYPOKALEMIC METABOLIC ALKALOSIS with volume depletion. (Aldosterone and hypovolemia cause renal paradox: distal tubule wastes K+ and H+ in exchange for Na+, producing "paradoxical aciduria"). CRITICAL SURGICAL PRINCIPLE: PYLORIC STENOSIS IS A MEDICAL EMERGENCY, NOT A SURGICAL EMERGENCY! PYLOROMYOTOMY MUST NEVER BE PERFORMED IMMEDIATELY! The infant MUST BE RESUSCITATED WITH IV ISOTONIC FLUIDS (Normal Saline + Dextrose and Potassium) to normalize electrolytes, chloride (> 100), and bicarbonate (< 28) BEFORE ANESTHESIA AND SURGERY (prevents postoperative central apnea and arrhythmias). Definitive surgery: Ramstedt pyloromyotomy.
necessaryInference: Identify hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, and recognize that intravenous isotonic fluid and electrolyte correction must completely precede surgical pyloromyotomy to avoid life-threatening anesthetic complications.
strongestDistractor: Immediate emergent laparoscopic pyloromyotomy within 2 hours of ultrasound confirmation to prevent gastric rupture
distractorExclusion: Pyloric stenosis is not a surgical emergency; operating on an infant with severe hypochloremic alkalosis causes fatal anesthetic central hypoventilation/apnea. Medical fluid resuscitation must completely precede surgery.

references.label: Ranells S, Carver D, Kirby R. Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. Semin Pediatr Surg. 2021;30(5):151101. PMID: 34794695.

subject: Pediatrics
topic: Meckel Diverticulum Technetium-99m Pertechnetate Scintigraphy Diagnosis
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Meckel Diverticulum: Most common congenital gastrointestinal anomaly. Embryology: Failure of the VITELLINE DUCT (omphalomesenteric duct) to completely obliterate during week 7-8. Anatomy: TRUE DIVERTICULUM (contains ALL THREE LAYERS: mucosa, submucosa, muscularis propria). Rule of 2s: 2% of population, 2 inches long, within 2 feet of ileocecal valve, 2 types of ectopic tissue (GASTRIC MUCOSA [~80-85%] and PANCREATIC TISSUE), manifests before 2 years of age. CLINICAL PRESENTATION: PAINLESS, BRISK, MASSIVE LOWER GASTROINTESTINAL BLEEDING (melena or bright red/maroon hematochezia) in a young toddler (< 2-3 years old). Pathophysiology of bleeding: The ECTOPIC GASTRIC MUCOSA secretes hydrochloric acid, which ulcerates the adjacent NORMAL, UNPROTECTED ILEAL MUCOSA. Can also serve as a lead point for intussusception or volvulus. DIAGNOSTIC TEST OF CHOICE: TECHNETIUM-99M PERTECHNETATE SCINTIGRAPHY ("MECKEL SCAN"): 99mTc-pertechnetate is selectively taken up by the sodium-iodide symporter in GASTRIC PARIETAL CELLS, highlighting ectopic gastric mucosa in the right lower quadrant. Treatment: Surgical resection.
necessaryInference: Identify Meckel diverticulum in a toddler presenting with painless rectal bleeding, and deduce that Technetium-99m pertechnetate scan identifies ectopic gastric mucosa that ulcerates adjacent ileal tissue.
strongestDistractor: Colonoscopy with biopsy demonstrating extensive pseudomembranous mucosal ulcerations
distractorExclusion: Colonoscopy is not first-line and pseudomembranes indicate C. difficile; painless gross hematochezia in an otherwise well toddler is the classic presentation of Meckel diverticulum, diagnosed via Technetium-99m pertechnetate scan.

references.label: Blumenkrantz MJ, Ramzy AI. Meckel diverticulum. Pediatr Rev. 2018;39(11):564-566. PMID: 30385627.

subject: Pediatrics
topic: Severe Combined Immunodeficiency SCID Newborn Screening TRECs
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID): Genetic defect causing profound deficiency of BOTH T CELLS AND B CELLS. Genetics: 1. X-linked recessive (most common, ~50%): Mutation in IL-2RG (common gamma chain of cytokine receptors IL-2, IL-4, IL-7, IL-9, IL-15, IL-21; IL-7 defect halts T-cell development). 2. Autosomal recessive: ADENOSINE DEAMINASE (ADA) DEFICIENCY (toxic dATP accumulation kills lymphocytes) or RAG1/RAG2 defects (V(D)J recombination failure). Clinical presentation: INFANT < 6 MONTHS with severe, recurrent, life-threatening opportunistic infections (Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, Candida thrush refractory to nystatin, CMV, chronic viral diarrhea, failure to thrive). Exam/Labs: ABSENT THYMIC SHADOW on CXR, ABSENT TONSILS AND LYMPH NODES, PROFOUND LYMPHOPENIA (absolute lymphocyte count < 1,500/mm3). Flow cytometry: Markedly reduced/absent CD3+ T cells. NEWBORN SCREENING: MEASUREMENT OF T-CELL RECEPTOR EXCISION CIRCLES (TRECs) in dried blood spots. Low/absent TRECs indicates lack of thymic T-cell maturation. MANAGEMENT: MEDICAL EMERGENCY! STRICT ISOLATION; IRRADIATED, LEUKOREDUCED, CMV-NEGATIVE BLOOD PRODUCTS ONLY; NO LIVE VACCINES (rotavirus, MMR, varicella, BCG). DEFINITIVE CURATIVE TREATMENT: ALLOGENEIC HEMATOPOIETIC STEM CELL TRANSPLANTATION (HSCT) ideally before 3.5 months of age.
necessaryInference: Recognize Severe Combined Immunodeficiency by absent thymic shadow, severe lymphopenia, and opportunistic infections, and deduce that newborn screening measures T-cell receptor excision circles (TRECs) and definitive curative therapy is urgent hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.
strongestDistractor: Immediate initiation of monthly intravenous immunoglobulin infusions as definitive curative lifelong therapy
distractorExclusion: IVIG replaces antibodies but does not restore defective cellular (T-cell) immunity; allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is the only curative treatment for SCID.

references.label: Haddad E, Logan BR, Griffith LM, et al. SCID genotype and approach to analysis of outcomes in primary immune deficiency treatment consortium. J Allergy Clin Immunol. 2018;141(5):1848-1857. PMID: 29199161.

subject: Pediatrics
topic: Kawasaki Disease Diagnostic Criteria and IVIG Treatment to Prevent Aneurysms
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Kawasaki Disease (Mucocutaneous Lymph Node Syndrome): Medium-vessel necrotizing vasculitis with marked predilection for CORONARY ARTERIES. Epidemiology: Asian descent, age < 5 years (peak 18-24 months). DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA: FEVER FOR >= 5 DAYS PLUS AT LEAST 4 OF THE FOLLOWING 5 CRITERIA (Mnemonic: "CRASH and Burn"): 1. Conjunctivitis (bilateral, bulbar, non-exudative, spares limbus). 2. Rash (polymorphous, maculopapular/erythematous, trunk/perineum). 3. Adenopathy (cervical, usually unilateral, > 1.5 cm, non-tender). 4. Strawberry tongue / oral changes (erythema of lips, lip cracking/fissuring, strawberry tongue). 5. Hand/foot changes (erythema and indurated non-pitting edema of palms/soles; periungual desquamation in convalescent phase). COMPLICATION: CORONARY ARTERY ANEURYSMS (develops in 20-25% of untreated children; risk of myocardial infarction and rupture!). TREATMENT: 1. INTRAVENOUS IMMUNOGLOBULIN (IVIG, single high-dose 2 g/kg within first 10 days of fever). 2. HIGH-DOSE ORAL ASPIRIN (anti-inflammatory dose 80-100 mg/kg/day during acute phase, switched to low-dose antiplatelet 3-5 mg/kg/day once afebrile). 3. ECHOCARDIOGRAM at baseline, 2 weeks, and 6-8 weeks.
necessaryInference: Identify Kawasaki disease by fever >= 5 days and 4 classic clinical criteria, and deduce that immediate single-dose IVIG combined with aspirin is mandatory within 10 days of onset to prevent life-threatening coronary artery aneurysms.
strongestDistractor: Immediate administration of high-dose pulsed intravenous methylprednisolone without immunoglobulin or aspirin
distractorExclusion: First-line therapy for Kawasaki disease is high-dose IVIG plus aspirin; corticosteroids are reserved as adjuvant therapy for IVIG-resistant disease.

references.label: McCrindle BW, Rowley AH, Newburger JW, et al. Diagnosis, Treatment, and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease: A Scientific Statement for Health Professionals From the American Heart Association. Circulation. 2017;135(17):e927-e999. PMID: 28356445.

subject: Pediatrics
topic: Chronic Granulomatous Disease Catalase-Positive Infections and DHR Assay
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD): Genetic deficiency in NADPH OXIDASE (CYBB gene mutation, X-linked recessive in ~70%; autosomal recessive in ~30%). Normal function: NADPH oxidase generates superoxide (O2-) from molecular oxygen to drive the respiratory burst in neutrophils and macrophages. Consequence of defect: Phagocytes can engulf bacteria, but CANNOT GENERATE SUPEROXIDE OR HYDROGEN PEROXIDE TO KILL INTRACELLULAR PATHOGENS. PATHOGENS: Susceptible specifically to CATALASE-POSITIVE ORGANISMS (mnemonic "SPACE": Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas/Burkholderia cepacia, Aspergillus, Nocardia, Serratia marcescens). Catalase-positive microbes break down their own endogenous H2O2, depriving the phagocyte of any peroxide to convert to hypochlorite (HOCl). Catalase-negative organisms (e.g., Streptococcus) generate H2O2 that the host myeloperoxidase can use to kill them! DIAGNOSTIC TEST OF CHOICE: DIHYDRORHODAMINE (DHR) 123 FLOW CYTOMETRY ASSAY (demonstrates absence of green fluorescence oxidation; replaces the obsolete nitroblue tetrazolium NBT slide test). PROPHYLAXIS: Lifelong daily oral TRIMETHOPRIM-SULFAMETHOXAZOLE (TMP-SMX, covers S. aureus, Burkholderia, Nocardia, Serratia) + ITRACONAZOLE (covers Aspergillus) + SUBCUTANEOUS INTERFERON-GAMMA (IFN-gamma). Curative: Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.
necessaryInference: Synthesize that recurrent lymphadenitis and liver abscesses from catalase-positive organisms (Serratia, S. aureus) indicate Chronic Granulomatous Disease, diagnosed via dihydrorhodamine-123 flow cytometry and managed with lifelong TMP-SMX and itraconazole prophylaxis.
strongestDistractor: Nitroblue tetrazolium reduction slide test as the preferred modern confirmatory assay, followed by monthly intravenous immunoglobulin infusions
distractorExclusion: NBT slide test is obsolete and qualitative; DHR flow cytometry is the modern quantitative standard. IVIG is ineffective because CGD is a phagocyte oxidative defect, not a humoral antibody deficiency.

references.label: Rider NL, Jameson MB, Creech CB. Chronic Granulomatous Disease: Epidemiology, Pathophysiology, and Genetic Basis of Disease. J Pediatric Infect Dis Soc. 2018;7(Suppl 1):S2-S5. PMID: 29741634.

subject: Pediatrics
topic: Henoch-Schonlein Purpura IgA Vasculitis Clinical Tetrad and Complications
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Henoch-Schonlein Purpura (HSP / IgA Vasculitis): Most common systemic vasculitis of childhood (peak age 3 to 10 years), frequently following an upper respiratory tract infection. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Deposition of IgA-ANTIGEN IMMUNE COMPLEXES in the walls of small arterioles, capillaries, and venules, triggering leukocytoclastic vasculitis. CLASSIC CLINICAL TETRAD: 1. PALPABLE PURPURA: Symmetrical, non-blanching, raised purpuric papules distributed predominantly over DEPENDENT AREAS: BUTTOCKS AND LOWER EXTREMITIES (extensor surfaces), sparing trunk. CRITICAL LAB FINDING: NORMAL OR ELEVATED PLATELET COUNT! (Purpura without thrombocytopenia rules out ITP/TTP). 2. ARTHRITIS / ARTHRALGIAS: Non-deforming, migratory oligoarthritis of knees and ankles. 3. GASTROINTESTINAL INVOLVEMENT: Colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, occult or gross hematochezia. MAJOR GI COMPLICATION: ILEOILEAL OR ILEOCOLIC INTUSSUSCEPTION (caused by intramural bowel wall hematoma acting as a lead point!). 4. RENAL DISEASE: IgA NEPHROPATHY (hematuria, proteinuria, RBC casts). MANAGEMENT: Supportive care (hydration, NSAIDs for joint pain). Systemic corticosteroids (prednisone) for severe abdominal pain or glomerulonephritis.
necessaryInference: Identify Henoch-Schonlein purpura by lower extremity palpable purpura with normal platelets, abdominal pain, and arthralgias, and recognize the risk of intussusception and renal disease while managing supportively.
strongestDistractor: Immediate administration of high-dose intravenous immunoglobulin and antiplatelet aspirin therapy to prevent coronary arteritis
distractorExclusion: IVIG and aspirin are the treatment for Kawasaki disease; Henoch-Schonlein purpura is an IgA vasculitis managed supportively, with normal coronary arteries.

references.label: Reamy BV, Servey JT, Williams PM. Henoch-Schonlein Purpura (IgA Vasculitis): Rapid Evidence Review. Am Fam Physician. 2020;102(4):229-233. PMID: 32803922.

subject: Pediatrics
topic: Sickle Cell Disease Acute Chest Syndrome Diagnostic Criteria and Management
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Sickle Cell Acute Chest Syndrome (ACS): LEADING CAUSE OF MORTALITY IN SICKLE CELL DISEASE. Pathophysiology: Vaso-occlusion of pulmonary microvasculature triggered by INFECTION (atypical bacteria like Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae; viral pathogens), FAT EMBOLISM (from necrotic bone marrow during vaso-occlusive crisis), or hypoventilation/atelectasis. DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA: A NEW PULMONARY INFILTRATE ON CHEST RADIOGRAPH INVOLVING AT LEAST ONE COMPLETE LUNG SEGMENT, PLUS AT LEAST ONE OF THE FOLLOWING: 1. Fever (temp >= 38.5 C). 2. Hypoxemia (pulse oximetry drop > 3% from baseline, or PaO2 < 60 mm Hg). 3. Tachypnea, intercostal retractions, or cough. 4. Chest pain. IMMEDIATE MANAGEMENT BUNDLE: 1. Oxygen therapy (maintain SpO2 >= 92-95%). 2. EMPIRIC BROAD-SPECTRUM IV ANTIBIOTICS: CEPHALOSPORIN (Ceftriaxone / Cefotaxime) PLUS A MACROLIDE (Azithromycin) to cover encapsulated bacteria (S. pneumoniae) AND atypical pathogens (Mycoplasma). 3. Judicious, gentle IV hydration (avoid overhydration -> pulmonary edema!). 4. Incentive spirometry and multimodal pain control. INDICATION FOR URGENT SIMPLE VS EXCHANGE TRANSFUSION: SIMPLE TRANSFUSION: For moderate disease with falling Hb, keep Hb < 10-11 g/dL (prevent hyperviscosity). URGENT EXCHANGE TRANSFUSION (erythrocytapheresis): Indicated for SEVERE / RAPIDLY PROGRESSIVE ACS (severe hypoxemia PaO2 < 60, multi-lobar infiltrates, altered mental status, hemodynamically unstable) to rapidly reduce HbS fraction to < 30%.
necessaryInference: Identify Acute Chest Syndrome in sickle cell disease by new pulmonary infiltrate and hypoxemia, and deduce that immediate management requires empiric ceftriaxone plus azithromycin, cautious hydration, and urgent exchange transfusion if severe respiratory compromise occurs.
strongestDistractor: Immediate aggressive intravenous fluid boluses of 60 mL/kg normal saline to restore intravascular volume, followed by high-dose oral corticosteroids
distractorExclusion: Aggressive fluid boluses precipitate acute pulmonary edema in sickled pulmonary vasculature; corticosteroids are avoided in ACS because they trigger severe rebound vaso-occlusive crises.

references.label: Howard J, Hart N, Roberts-Harewood M, et al. Guideline on the management of acute chest syndrome in sickle cell disease. Br J Haematol. 2015;169(4):492-505. PMID: 25772390.

subject: Pediatrics
topic: Sickle Cell Splenic Sequestration Crisis Pathophysiology and Emergency Transfusion
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Sickle Cell Anemia Acute Hematologic Crises: 1. SPLENIC SEQUESTRATION CRISIS: Occurs in young children (age 6 months to 4 years) BEFORE the spleen undergoes complete autosplenectomy from repeated infarctions. Pathophysiology: Massive intra-splenic trapping/pooling of sickled erythrocytes within splenic red pulp cords and sinusoids. Clinical presentation: SUDDEN, SEVERE PALLOR, LETHARGY, HYPOTENSIVE SHOCK, and a RAPIDLY ENLARGING, EXQUISITELY TENDER, MASSIVE SPLEEN. Labs: PRECIPITOUS DROP IN HEMOGLOBIN (often < 4 g/dL), severe thrombocytopenia (platelets trapped in spleen), BUT MARKED RETICULOCYTOSIS (> 10-20%; bone marrow is hyperactive, trying to compensate!). CRITICAL EMERGENCY MANAGEMENT: Judicious, CAUTIOUS SMALL-VOLUME PACKED RBC TRANSFUSION (5-10 mL/kg slowly) to restore hemodynamics. WARNING: DO NOT OVER-TRANSFUSE! As the child stabilizes, the sequestered red cells AUTOTRANSFUSE back from the decompressing spleen into the circulation; over-transfusion causes FATAL HYPERVISCOSITY SYNDROME! Splenectomy is indicated after stabilization due to high recurrence (> 50%). 2. CONTRAST WITH APLASTIC CRISIS (Parvovirus B19): Severe drop in hemoglobin, BUT RETICULOCYTE COUNT DROPS TO NEAR ZERO (< 0.5% / absent reticulocytes!), and spleen is NOT enlarged.
necessaryInference: Contrast splenic sequestration crisis (massive splenomegaly, reticulocytosis, hypotensive shock) from aplastic crisis (reticulocytopenia, no splenomegaly) in a toddler with sickle cell disease, requiring cautious small-volume transfusion to avoid post-decompression hyperviscosity.
strongestDistractor: Immediate emergent splenectomy within 2 hours of presentation while the patient remains in profound hypotensive shock
distractorExclusion: Emergency surgery in profound unresuscitated shock carries extreme mortality; the child must be stabilized first with cautious transfusion, with elective splenectomy performed after recovery to prevent recurrence.

references.label: Brousse V, Buffet P, Rees D. The spleen and sickle cell disease: the sick(led) spleen. Br J Haematol. 2014;166(2):165-176. PMID: 24862308.
