subject: Pediatrics
topic: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis SCFE Emergency Pinning in Situ
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis (SCFE): Displacement of the femoral epiphysis from the femoral neck through the hypertrophic zone of the physeal growth plate. Epidemiology: OBESE ADOLESCENTS (age 11-14 in boys, 10-13 in girls; male predominance; also associated with hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency). Clinical presentation: Insidious onset of dull, achy hip, groin, thigh, or REFERRED KNEE PAIN (up to 25% of patients present ONLY with knee or thigh pain; EXAMINE THE HIP IN EVERY ADOLESCENT WITH KNEE PAIN!). Examination: Antalgic or waddling gait; OBLIGATORY EXTERNAL ROTATION OF THE HIP WHEN THE HIP IS PASSIVELY FLEXED (Drehmann sign); decreased internal rotation, abduction, and flexion. DIAGNOSTIC IMAGING: ANTEROPOSTERIOR (AP) AND FROG-LEG LATERAL RADIOGRAPHS OF BOTH HIPS (demonstrates posterior and medial displacement of the femoral head relative to the femoral neck; "ice cream slipping off the cone"; Klein line does not intersect the lateral epiphysis). CRITICAL MANAGEMENT STEP: 1. IMMEDIATE STRICT NON-WEIGHT-BEARING (wheelchair/crutches) to prevent acute catastrophic progression and avascular necrosis. 2. URGENT SURGICAL INTERNAL FIXATION WITH A SINGLE CANNULATED SCREW (PINNING IN SITU). Do NOT attempt closed reduction (closed reduction causes osteonecrosis / avascular necrosis!).
necessaryInference: Identify SCFE in an obese adolescent presenting with referred knee pain and external rotation on hip flexion, and recognize that immediate strict non-weight-bearing and urgent surgical pinning in situ are mandatory to prevent avascular necrosis.
strongestDistractor: Immediate closed manual reduction under conscious sedation followed by application of a bilateral hip spica cast
distractorExclusion: Closed reduction is strictly contraindicated in SCFE because manipulation disrupts the delicate retinacular blood vessels, causing avascular necrosis of the femoral head; treatment is urgent percutaneous screw fixation in situ.

references.label: Peck D. Slipped capital femoral epiphysis: diagnosis for the primary care provider. Am Fam Physician. 2010;82(3):258-262. PMID: 20672790.

subject: Pediatrics
topic: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip Barlow and Ortolani and Pavlik Harness
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip (DDH): Spectrum of abnormal hip development (acetabular dysplasia, subluxation, dislocation). RISK FACTORS: Breech presentation (strongest risk factor!), female sex (6:1), family history, tight swaddling. PHYSICAL EXAM MANEUVERS: 1. BARLOW MANEUVER: Flex hip to 90 degrees and ADDUCT with gentle posterior pressure -> pushes femoral head OUT of acetabulum ("Barlow dislocates Backwards"). 2. ORTOLANI MANEUVER: Flex hip to 90 degrees and ABDUCT while lifting greater trochanter anteriorly -> reduces dislocated femoral head back into acetabulum with a palpable "clunk" ("Ortolani Out and in"). Galeazzi sign (unequal knee heights when hips/knees flexed) and asymmetric thigh skin folds in older infants. IMAGING MODALITY OF CHOICE: 1. INFANT < 4 TO 6 MONTHS: HIP ULTRASONOGRAPHY (the femoral head and acetabulum are cartilaginous and unossified; radiographs are uninterpretable!). 2. INFANT > 4 TO 6 MONTHS: AP PELVIC RADIOGRAPHS (femoral head ossific nucleus appears). TREATMENT: For infants < 6 months with confirmed DDH: PAVLIK HARNESS (dynamic flexion and abduction splint that centers the femoral head in the acetabulum to stimulate normal acetabular remodeling).
necessaryInference: Identify developmental dysplasia of the hip by positive Ortolani/Barlow maneuvers, and recognize that hip ultrasound is the diagnostic imaging modality of choice in infants under 4-6 months, managed with a Pavlik harness.
strongestDistractor: Immediate anteroposterior pelvic radiography to assess the acetabular angle and teardrop distance
distractorExclusion: Pelvic radiographs are uninterpretable in infants under 4-6 months because the femoral head is predominantly radiolucent cartilage; ultrasound is the mandatory modality for early infancy.

references.label: Shaw BA, Segal LS. Evaluation and Referral for Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip in Infants. Pediatrics. 2016;138(6):e20163107. PMID: 27940743.

subject: Pediatrics
topic: Septic Arthritis vs Transient Synovitis Kocher Criteria and Arthrocentesis
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Septic Arthritis vs Transient Synovitis of the Hip: Both present with acute hip pain and limp in young children (age 2 to 6). 1. TRANSIENT SYNOVITIS (toxic synovitis): Benign, self-limiting post-viral reactive inflammation of synovial lining. Child is non-toxic, afebrile or low-grade temp, walks with an antalgic limp, normal or mildly elevated inflammatory markers. Ultrasound shows small effusion. Treated with REST AND NSAIDs (resolves in 1-2 weeks). 2. SEPTIC ARTHRITIS: BACTERIAL INFECTION of joint space (S. aureus, S. pyogenes, S. pneumoniae; K. kingae in < 3 years). Orthopedic emergency! Causes irreversible cartilage destruction and avascular necrosis within hours. Child is toxic, high fever, REFUSES TO BEAR ANY WEIGHT, holds hip in flexion, abduction, and external rotation; any passive motion causes agonizing pain. KOCHER CRITERIA (Predicts Septic Arthritis probability): 1. Fever > 38.5 C. 2. Inability to bear weight on the affected limb. 3. ESR > 40 mm/hr (or CRP > 20 mg/L). 4. Serum WBC > 12,000/mm3. SCORING: 0 criteria = < 0.2% probability; 1 = 3%; 2 = 40%; 3 = 93%; 4 = 99% probability of septic arthritis! MANAGEMENT IF >= 3 CRITERIA: URGENT ULTRASOUND-GUIDED ARTHROCENTESIS (synovial fluid WBC > 50,000/mm3 with > 75% neutrophils confirms septic arthritis) followed by IMMEDIATE SURGICAL IRRIGATION AND DEBRIDEMENT (arthrotomy) and IV antibiotics.
necessaryInference: Apply the Kocher criteria to an acutely limping child with high fever, non-weight-bearing, elevated ESR and leukocytosis, and deduce that urgent arthrocentesis and surgical drainage are indicated for high-probability septic arthritis.
strongestDistractor: Reassurance, prescription of oral ibuprofen, and scheduled outpatient reassessment in 48 hours for transient synovitis
distractorExclusion: The child meets all 4 Kocher criteria (99% probability of septic arthritis); treating with NSAIDs alone will result in rapid, irreversible destruction of the femoral head cartilage and osteonecrosis.

references.label: Kocher MS, Zurakowski D, Kasser JR. Differentiating between septic arthritis and transient synovitis of the hip in children: an evidence-based clinical prediction algorithm. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 1999;81(12):1662-1670. PMID: 10608376.

subject: Pediatrics
topic: Croup Laryngotracheobronchitis Dexamethasone and Racemic Epinephrine
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Upper Airway Emergencies in Children: 1. CROUP (Laryngotracheobronchitis): Parainfluenza virus (types 1 and 2). Age 6 months to 3 years. Presentation: Viral prodrome (rhinorrhea, low fever) followed by "BARKING" SEAL-LIKE COUGH, hoarseness, and INSPIRATORY STRIDOR. X-ray: AP neck radiograph shows subglottic tracheal narrowing ("STEEPLE SIGN"). MANAGEMENT BASED ON STRIDOR: (a) Mild (barking cough, NO stridor at rest): SINGLE DOSE OF ORAL DEXAMETHASONE (0.15 to 0.6 mg/kg) + humidified air/mist. (b) Moderate to Severe (INSPIRATORY STRIDOR AT REST, retractions, agitation): NEBULIZED RACEMIC EPINEPHRINE (causes alpha-1 arteriolar vasoconstriction in subglottic mucosa, rapidly shrinking edema) PLUS SINGLE-DOSE ORAL/IM/IV DEXAMETHASONE. Observe for 2-4 hours post-epinephrine for "rebound stridor" before discharge. 2. EPIGLOTTITIS: H. influenzae type b or Strep/Staph. Sudden high fever, "hot potato" voice, DROOLING, TRIPOD POSITION, "thumbprint sign" on lateral neck X-ray. DO NOT AGITATE; secure airway in OR! 3. BACTERIAL TRACHEITIS: S. aureus superinfection following croup; toxic, high fever, purulent tracheal secretions, fail to respond to racemic epinephrine.
necessaryInference: Identify moderate-to-severe croup by barking cough and inspiratory stridor at rest with subglottic narrowing (steeple sign), and deduce that management requires immediate nebulized racemic epinephrine combined with systemic dexamethasone.
strongestDistractor: Immediate transfer to the operating room for direct rigid laryngoscopy and endotracheal intubation
distractorExclusion: Immediate intubation in the OR is the management for acute epiglottitis (drooling, tripod position, toxic); croup with stridor at rest is managed with nebulized racemic epinephrine and dexamethasone.

references.label: Smith DK, McDermott AJ, Sullivan JF. Croup: Diagnosis and Management. Am Fam Physician. 2018;97(9):575-580. PMID: 29763253.

subject: Pediatrics
topic: Foreign Body Aspiration Asymmetric Air Trapping and Rigid Bronchoscopy
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Foreign Body Aspiration (FBA): Most common in toddlers age 1 to 3 years (organic items: peanuts, seeds, popcorn, hot dogs, small toy parts). Anatomy: RIGHT MAINSTEM BRONCHUS is more common in older children/adults (wider, more vertical, larger diameter), but roughly equal in toddlers. Clinical: Sudden choking, coughing, or gagging episode while eating or playing, followed by UNILATERAL WHEEZING, ASYMMETRIC BREATH SOUNDS, or persistent focal atelectasis/pneumonia refractory to antibiotics. RADIOGRAPHIC EVALUATION: Standard AP and lateral chest radiographs may be normal (most organic objects are radiolucent!). DIAGNOSTIC RADIOGRAPHIC MODALITY: INSPIRATORY AND EXPIRATORY (OR BILATERAL DECUBITUS) CHEST RADIOGRAPHS: Foreign body creates a "BALL-VALVE" EFFECT (air enters during inspiration when bronchus expands, but gets trapped during expiration when bronchus constricts). Findings on expiration: UNILATERAL HYPERLUCENCY AND HYPEREXPANSION OF THE AFFECTED LUNG, with MEDIASTINAL SHIFT TO THE CONTRALATERAL (NORMAL) SIDE! GOLD STANDARD DEFINITIVE PROCEDURE: RIGID BRONCHOSCOPY under general anesthesia (both diagnostic and therapeutic; rigid allows better optical control and foreign body extraction instruments than flexible bronchoscopy).
necessaryInference: Synthesize that sudden choking followed by asymmetric wheezing represents foreign body aspiration, diagnosed by expiratory air trapping and hyperlucency with contralateral mediastinal shift, and managed with urgent rigid bronchoscopy.
strongestDistractor: Flexible fiberoptic bronchoscopy under local topical anesthesia in the outpatient pulmonary clinic
distractorExclusion: Flexible bronchoscopy has inadequate airway control and grasping instruments for foreign body retrieval; rigid bronchoscopy under general anesthesia is the gold standard.

references.label: Cramer N, Jabbour N, Tavarez MM, Taylor RS. Foreign Body Aspiration. StatPearls. 2023. PMID: 30252328.

subject: Pediatrics
topic: Neonatal Respiratory Distress Syndrome Surfactant Deficiency and CPAP
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Neonatal Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS / Hyaline Membrane Disease): Most common cause of respiratory failure in PREMATURE INFANTS (< 32 weeks, inversely proportional to gestational age; peak risk < 28 weeks). Pathophysiology: DEFICIENCY OF PULMONARY SURFACTANT, synthesized by TYPE II PNEUMOCYTES starting at week 24, but reaching mature levels after week 35. Surfactant component: DIPALMITOYLPHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (lecithin; L/S ratio > 2.0 indicates lung maturity). Function: Lowers alveolar surface tension (Law of Laplace: P = 2T/r). Lack of surfactant causes: HIGH ALVEOLAR SURFACE TENSION -> DIFFUSE MICROATELECTASIS, hypoxemia, ventilation-perfusion mismatch, and formation of fibrin-rich "hyaline membranes." Risk factors: Prematurity, MATERNAL DIABETES (maternal hyperglycemia -> fetal hyperinsulinemia; INSULIN DIRECTLY BLOCKS SURFACTANT TRANSCRIPTION!), male sex, cesarean delivery without labor. Presentation: Tachypnea, grunting, nasal flaring, intercostal retractions within minutes of birth. CHEST RADIOGRAPH: UNIFORM "GROUND-GLASS" RETICULOGRANULAR OPACITIES WITH PROMINENT AIR BRONCHOGRAMS and low lung volumes. TREATMENT: 1. Non-invasive respiratory support: NASAL CPAP (Continuous Positive Airway Pressure) as initial preferred strategy. 2. EXOGENOUS SURFACTANT REPLACEMENT via endotracheal instillation for infants failing CPAP.
necessaryInference: Identify neonatal RDS by ground-glass reticulogranular infiltrates and air bronchograms in a premature infant of a diabetic mother, and recognize that initial management is nasal CPAP with endotracheal surfactant administration.
strongestDistractor: Immediate high-frequency chest wall oscillation and intravenous furosemide to clear retained alveolar fetal lung fluid
distractorExclusion: Clearing retained fetal lung fluid with fluid reabsorption describes Transient Tachypnea of the Newborn (TTN), which presents with fluid in interlobar fissures in term infants; RDS is caused by surfactant deficiency with ground-glass opacities requiring CPAP and surfactant.

references.label: Sweet DG, Carnielli V, Greisen G, et al. European Consensus Guidelines on the Management of Respiratory Distress Syndrome - 2019 Update. Neonatology. 2019;115(4):432-446. PMID: 30974433.

subject: Pediatrics
topic: Infant of Diabetic Mother Hypoglycemia and Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Infant of Diabetic Mother (IDM) pathophysiology: Maternal hyperglycemia -> crosses placenta (glucose crosses via GLUT1). FETAL PANCREAS RESPONDS BY DEVELOPING ISLET CELL HYPERPLASIA AND MASSIVE HYPERINSULINEMIA (Insulin DOES NOT cross the placenta!). Consequences of fetal hyperinsulinemia: 1. MACROSOMIA (large for gestational age > 4,000 g; insulin is a potent fetal growth factor; risk of shoulder dystocia / clavicle fracture / Erb palsy). 2. ACUTE NEONATAL HYPOGLYCEMIA: At delivery, maternal glucose supply is abruptly severed, but the neonate hyperplastic beta-cells continue to pump high insulin -> SEVERE HYPOGLYCEMIA within 1 to 2 hours of birth! 3. TRANSIENT HYPERTROPHIC CARDIOMYOPATHY: Insulin stimulates massive GLYCOGEN AND FAT DEPOSITION IN THE INTERVENTRICULAR SEPTUM -> asymmetric septal hypertrophy causing dynamic left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction. Management: BETA-BLOCKERS (propranolol) if symptomatic; REGRESSES SPONTANEOUSLY within 3-6 months as insulin normalizes! 4. Hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, polycythemia (fetal hypoxia -> high EPO -> risk of renal vein thrombosis), and neonatal RDS (insulin inhibits surfactant).
necessaryInference: Synthesize that infants of diabetic mothers experience acute neonatal hypoglycemia due to islet hyperplasia, and transient hypertrophic cardiomyopathy due to insulin-driven glycogen deposition in the interventricular septum, which resolves spontaneously over several months.
strongestDistractor: Permanent autosomal dominant sarcomeric beta-myosin heavy chain mutation requiring lifelong implantable defibrillator placement
distractorExclusion: Familial HCM is genetic and permanent; IDM hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is a transient metabolic phenomenon driven by fetal hyperinsulinism that resolves spontaneously within 3 to 6 months.

references.label: Nold JL, Georgieff MK. Infants of diabetic mothers. Pediatr Clin North Am. 2004;51(3):619-637. PMID: 15157588.

subject: Pediatrics
topic: Neonatal Sepsis Empiric Antibiotics and Ceftriaxone Contraindication
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Neonatal Sepsis (< 28 days of life): Early-onset (< 72 hours, intrapartum vertical transmission) vs Late-onset (> 72 hours, hospital/community acquired). THREE MAJOR EARLY-ONSET PATHOGENS: 1. GROUP B STREPTOCOCCUS (Streptococcus agalactiae, #1 cause). 2. ESCHERICHIA COLI (#2 cause, most common in premature infants). 3. LISTERIA MONOCYTOGENES (facultative intracellular Gram-positive rod). EMPIRIC FIRST-LINE ANTIBIOTIC REGIMEN: INTRAVENOUS AMPICILLIN PLUS GENTAMICIN (or Ampicillin plus Cefotaxime). WHY AMPICILLIN? Ampicillin provides mandatory bactericidal coverage against LISTERIA MONOCYTOGENES and Group B Strep. (Cephalosporins have ZERO activity against Listeria!). WHY IS CEFTRIAXONE STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED IN NEONATES? 1. Ceftriaxone displaces bilirubin from serum albumin, markedly increasing free unconjugated bilirubin, causing BILIRUBIN ENCEPHALOPATHY / KERNICTERUS! 2. Ceftriaxone precipitates with intravenous calcium (forming insoluble calcium-ceftriaxone crystals in the lungs and kidneys, causing fatal organ failure). 3. Biliary sludging (ceftriaxone biliary pseudolithiasis). If a 3rd-generation cephalosporin is needed for meningitis, USE CEFOTAXIME, NEVER CEFTRIAXONE in neonates!
necessaryInference: Synthesize that neonatal sepsis empiric coverage requires ampicillin plus gentamicin (or cefotaxime) to cover GBS, E. coli, and Listeria, and recognize that ceftriaxone is strictly contraindicated in neonates due to albumin-bilirubin displacement and calcium precipitation.
strongestDistractor: Intravenous ceftriaxone plus vancomycin, because ceftriaxone achieves superior central nervous system penetration against Listeria
distractorExclusion: Cephalosporins have ZERO activity against Listeria, and ceftriaxone is strictly contraindicated in neonates due to albumin-bilirubin displacement causing kernicterus and calcium-ceftriaxone crystal precipitation.

references.label: Puopolo KM, Benitz WE, Zaoutis TE, et al. Management of Neonates Born at <=34 6/7 Weeks Gestation with Suspected or Proven Early-Onset Sepsis. Pediatrics. 2018;142(6):e20182896. PMID: 30455343.

subject: Pediatrics
topic: Pediatric Lead Toxicity Screening Venous Confirmation and Chelation
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Pediatric Lead Toxicity management: Sources: Lead-based paint in homes built BEFORE 1978 (peeling paint chips, lead dust during renovation), contaminated soil, imported ceramic cookware/lead-glazed pottery, traditional folk remedies (Greta, Azarcon). Pathophysiology: Inhibits FERROCHELATASE AND DELTA-AMINOLEVULINIC ACID (ALA) DEHYDRATASE, halting heme synthesis -> microcytic anemia with basophilic stippling on peripheral smear. Neurotoxicity: Irreversible cognitive impairment, developmental delay, hyperactivity, behavioral problems. SCREENING & DIAGNOSTIC RULES: 1. Initial screen: CAPILLARY FINGERSTICK BLOOD SAMPLE. (High false-positive rate due to environmental skin contamination!). 2. ANY ELEVATED CAPILLARY LEAD LEVEL (>= 5 mcg/dL) MUST BE CONFIRMED WITH A VENOUS BLOOD LEAD LEVEL (BLL)! 3. MANAGEMENT BASED ON VENOUS BLL: (a) BLL < 5 mcg/dL: Reassurance, normal. (b) BLL 5 to 44 mcg/dL: NO CHELATION! Environmental inspection, identify and remove lead source, dietary counseling (iron and calcium supplementation to block intestinal lead absorption), repeat BLL in 1-3 months. (c) BLL 45 to 69 mcg/dL: CHELATION THERAPY WITH ORAL SUCCIMER (DMSA / 2,3-dimercaptosuccinic acid). (d) BLL >= 70 mcg/dL (or acute encephalopathy): EMERGENCY INPATIENT ADMISSION! INTRAVENOUS CHELATION: DIMERCAPROL (BAL) FIRST, followed 4 hours later by IV CALCIUM DISODIUM EDTA (CaNa2EDTA). (BAL crosses blood-brain barrier; CaNa2EDTA is given after BAL to prevent lead redistribution into the central nervous system!).
necessaryInference: Synthesize pediatric lead management: confirm elevated capillary screening with venous blood lead level; manage levels 5-44 mcg/dL with environmental abatement and nutritional optimization; reserve oral succimer for levels 45-69 mcg/dL, and IV dimercaprol plus calcium EDTA for levels >= 70 mcg/dL.
strongestDistractor: Immediate administration of oral succimer chelation based directly on the initial elevated capillary blood lead screening result
distractorExclusion: Capillary screening has a high false-positive rate from skin contamination; chelation must NEVER be initiated without first confirming the elevation with a formal venous blood lead level.

references.label: Warniment ST, Tsang K, Galazka SS. Lead poisoning in children. Am Fam Physician. 2010;81(6):751-757. PMID: 20229973.

subject: Pediatrics
topic: Non-Accidental Trauma Child Abuse High-Specificity Skeletal Fractures
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Non-Accidental Trauma (NAT / Physical Child Abuse): Leading cause of traumatic infant mortality. FRACTURES WITH HIGH SPECIFICITY FOR ABUSE: 1. METAPHYSEAL CORNER FRACTURES / "BUCKET-HANDLE" FRACTURES: Planar microfractures across the primary spongiosa of the metaphysis caused by violent YANKING, TWISTING, OR FLUSHING OF EXTREMITIES. 2. POSTERIOR RIB FRACTURES: Caused by COMPRESSION / SQUEEZING OF THE INFANT THORAX during violent shaking (posterior ribs fracture against the transverse processes of the spine). Anterolateral rib fractures can occur from CPR, but POSTERIOR RIB FRACTURES ARE VIRTUALLY PATHOGNOMONIC FOR ABUSE! 3. Fractures of varying ages/stages of healing. 4. Complex skull fractures, scapular, spinous process, or sternal fractures in infants < 1 year. Other signs: Shaken baby syndrome (SUBDURAL HEMATOMA + RETINAL HEMORRHAGES), unexplained burns (scald burns with clear immersion lines, cigarette burns). MANDATORY NEXT STEPS: 1. ADMIT TO HOSPITAL for safety! 2. FULL SKELETAL SURVEY (X-rays of all bones) in children < 2 years. 3. NON-CONTRAST HEAD CT and OPHTHALMOLOGIC DILATED RETINAL EXAM. 4. MANDATORY IMMEDIATE REPORT TO CHILD PROTECTIVE SERVICES (CPS) / LAW ENFORCEMENT. (Physicians are legally mandated reporters; does NOT require parental consent or absolute proof!).
necessaryInference: Identify child abuse by posterior rib fractures and metaphyseal corner fractures inconsistent with developmental history, and recognize that mandatory actions include hospital admission, full skeletal survey, and immediate reporting to Child Protective Services.
strongestDistractor: Discharge the infant home with close outpatient follow-up while awaiting a formal genetics consultation for osteogenesis imperfecta
distractorExclusion: Discharging the infant places the child in immediate mortal danger; posterior rib and metaphyseal fractures are highly specific for abuse, and immediate hospitalization and CPS reporting are legally mandated.

references.label: Christian CW. The evaluation of suspected child physical abuse. Pediatrics. 2015;135(5):e1337-e1354. PMID: 25917988.

subject: Pediatrics
topic: Congenital Rubella Syndrome Triad vs Cytomegalovirus and Toxoplasmosis
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Congenital TORCH Infections: 1. CONGENITAL RUBELLA SYNDROME (Togavirus): CLASSIC TRIAD: (a) SENSORINEURAL HEARING LOSS (most common defect, ~80%). (b) CATARACTS (leukocoria / white pupillary reflex) or microphthalmia. (c) CARDIAC DEFECTS: PATENT DUCTUS ARTERIOSUS (PDA; continuous machine-like murmur at left infraclavicular area) or peripheral pulmonary artery stenosis. Additional signs: "BLUEBERRY MUFFIN" RASH (extramedullary hematopoiesis), microcephaly, radiolucent bone lesions ("celery stalk" metaphyses). Preventable by MATERNAL MMR VACCINE BEFORE PREGNANCY (live vaccine, contraindicated during pregnancy!). 2. CONGENITAL CYTOMEGALOVIRUS (CMV): Most common congenital viral infection. PERIVENTRICULAR INTRACRANIAL CALCIFICATIONS, microcephaly, sensorineural hearing loss, chorioretinitis. 3. CONGENITAL TOXOPLASMOSIS: Triad of CHORIORETINITIS, HYDROCEPHALUS, and DIFFUSE INTRACRANIAL CALCIFICATIONS (scattered in cortex, NOT periventricular!). Treat with pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine.
necessaryInference: Identify Congenital Rubella Syndrome by its classic triad of sensorineural hearing loss, cataracts, and continuous machine-like murmur of patent ductus arteriosus, accompanied by a blueberry muffin rash.
strongestDistractor: Congenital cytomegalovirus infection characterized by periventricular intracranial calcifications and microcephaly
distractorExclusion: CMV causes periventricular calcifications without congenital cataracts or patent ductus arteriosus; the triad of cataracts, PDA, and deafness is pathognomonic for Congenital Rubella Syndrome.

references.label: Lambert N, Strebel P, Orenstein W, et al. Rubella. Lancet. 2015;385(9984):2297-2307. PMID: 25576992.

subject: Medicine
topic: Septic Shock Resuscitation Hour-1 Bundle and Norepinephrine First-Line
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Sepsis and Septic Shock management (Surviving Sepsis Campaign Hour-1 Bundle): DEFINITIONS: Sepsis = life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection (SOFA score acute increase >= 2 points). Septic Shock = sepsis with PERSISTENT HYPOTENSION REQUIRING VASOPRESSORS to maintain MAP >= 65 mm Hg AND SERUM LACTATE > 2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation. HOUR-1 RESUSCITATION BUNDLE: 1. Measure serum lactate (remeasure within 2-4 hours if elevated). 2. OBTAIN BLOOD CULTURES PRIOR TO ANTIBIOTIC ADMINISTRATION (2 sets: aerobic and anaerobic; do not delay antibiotics > 45 minutes if cultures delayed). 3. ADMINISTER BROAD-SPECTRUM EMPIRIC IV ANTIMICROBIALS WITHIN 1 HOUR. 4. RAPID FLUID RESUSCITATION: Administer at least 30 mL/kg of IV BALANCED CRYSTALLOID (Lactated Ringer or Plasma-Lyte preferred over 0.9% saline to avoid hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis) within the first 3 hours for hypotension (MAP < 65) or lactate >= 4. 5. VASOPRESSOR OF CHOICE: NOREPINEPHRINE (potent alpha-1 vasoconstriction + mild beta-1 inotropy; superior to dopamine). Second-line add-on: VASOPRESSIN (fixed dose 0.03 units/min) to reduce norepinephrine requirements. Epinephrine is third-line.
necessaryInference: Synthesize the surviving sepsis Hour-1 bundle: obtain blood cultures before broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour, administer 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloids, and initiate norepinephrine as the first-line vasopressor for refractory hypotension to maintain MAP >= 65 mm Hg.
strongestDistractor: Immediate administration of high-dose dopamine infusion as first-line vasopressor and oral hydrocortisone prior to fluid boluses
distractorExclusion: Dopamine has higher tachyarrhythmia and mortality rates compared to norepinephrine; norepinephrine is the mandatory first-line vasopressor, and fluid resuscitation must precede steroids.

references.label: Evans L, Rhodes A, Alhazzani W, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2021. Crit Care Med. 2021;49(11):e1063-e1143. PMID: 34605781.

subject: Medicine
topic: Acute Bacterial Meningitis Empiric Regimen Age > 50 and Dexamethasone
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Acute Bacterial Meningitis empiric management: CORE TRIAD: Fever, headache, nuchal rigidity (meningismus: positive Kernig and Brudzinski signs) + altered mental status. EMPIRIC REGIMENS BASED ON AGE AND RISK: 1. ADULTS AGE 18 TO 50: VANCOMYCIN (covers cephalosporin-resistant S. pneumoniae) PLUS CEFTRIAXONE or CEFOTAXIME (covers N. meningitidis, S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae). 2. ADULTS AGE > 50, OR IMMUNOCOMPROMISED (alcoholism, malignancy, steroids, transplant): VANCOMYCIN + CEFTRIAXONE + AMPICILLIN! WHY AMPICILLIN? Ampicillin provides mandatory bactericidal coverage against LISTERIA MONOCYTOGENES (cephalosporins have zero activity against Listeria!). ADJUNCTIVE CORTICOSTEROIDS: INTRAVENOUS DEXAMETHASONE: Must be administered BEFORE OR CONCURRENTLY WITH THE FIRST DOSE OF ANTIBIOTICS. Why? Antibiotics cause rapid bacterial lysis, releasing massive cell wall fragments (peptidoglycan, teichoic acid, endotoxin) that trigger an explosive inflammatory cytokine burst in subarachnoid space. Dexamethasone reduces cerebral edema, elevated ICP, and PREVENTS SENSORINEURAL HEARING LOSS AND MORTALITY in Streptococcus pneumoniae meningitis. Discontinue dexamethasone if culture reveals N. meningitidis or Listeria.
necessaryInference: Synthesize bacterial meningitis empiric management in an adult over 50: administer vancomycin plus ceftriaxone plus ampicillin (to cover Listeria), combined with intravenous dexamethasone given prior to or with the first antibiotic dose to prevent neurological sequelae from pneumococcal lysis.
strongestDistractor: Vancomycin plus ceftriaxone monotherapy, administering dexamethasone only if the patient develops refractory seizures after 24 hours
distractorExclusion: Adults > 50 require ampicillin to cover Listeria monocytogenes; dexamethasone must be given BEFORE or WITH the first antibiotic dose, not delayed by 24 hours, to block initial lysis inflammation.

references.label: van de Beek D, Cabellos C, Dzupova O, et al. ESCMID guideline: diagnosis and treatment of acute bacterial meningitis. Clin Microbiol Infect. 2016;22 Suppl 3:S37-S62. PMID: 27062097.

subject: Medicine
topic: Cerebrospinal Fluid Analysis Bacterial vs Viral vs Fungal Meningitis
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF) Profiles: 1. ACUTE BACTERIAL MENINGITIS: OPENING PRESSURE: MARKEDLY ELEVATED (> 250 mm H2O). WBC COUNT: VERY HIGH (> 1,000 to 10,000/mm3) with PREDOMINANCE OF NEUTROPHILS / PMNs (> 80%). PROTEIN: MARKEDLY ELEVATED (> 100 to 500 mg/dL; disrupted blood-brain barrier). GLUCOSE: SEVERELY DEPRESSED (HYPOGLYCORRHACHIA: < 40 mg/dL, or CSF-to-serum glucose ratio < 0.4; bacteria and infiltrating leukocytes consume glucose via anaerobic glycolysis). 2. VIRAL (ASEPTIC) MENINGITIS (Enteroviruses, HSV): Opening pressure: Normal or mildly elevated. WBC: Mild elevation (10 to 500/mm3) with LYMPHOCYTIC PREDOMINANCE (early PMNs shift to lymphocytes within 24 h). Protein: Normal to mildly elevated (50-100 mg/dL). Glucose: COMPLETELY NORMAL (CSF/serum ratio > 0.6). 3. FUNGAL / TUBERCULOUS MENINGITIS (Cryptococcus, TB): Opening pressure: Markedly elevated (> 250-300). WBC: Moderate elevation (50 to 500/mm3) with LYMPHOCYTIC PREDOMINANCE. Protein: Extremely high (> 100-500). Glucose: SEVERELY DEPRESSED (< 40 mg/dL).
necessaryInference: Analyze CSF parameters to identify acute bacterial meningitis by its pathognomonic combination of high opening pressure (> 250), neutrophilic pleocytosis (> 1,000 cells with > 80% PMNs), marked hyperproteinorrhaica, and severe hypoglycorrhachia (CSF/serum ratio < 0.4).
strongestDistractor: Viral aseptic meningitis, characterized by a normal opening pressure, lymphocytic pleocytosis, and normal CSF glucose concentration
distractorExclusion: The CSF profile displays extreme neutrophilic pleocytosis (> 3,000 PMNs) with severe hypoglycorrhachia (< 20 mg/dL), which definitively establishes acute pyogenic bacterial meningitis, not viral.

references.label: Seehusen DA, Reeves MM, Fomin DA. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis. Am Fam Physician. 2003;68(6):1103-1108. PMID: 14524396.

subject: Medicine
topic: Cryptococcal Meningitis in HIV Induction and Serial Lumbar Punctures
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Cryptococcal Meningoencephalitis in HIV/AIDS (CD4 < 100/mm3): Clinical presentation: Subacute progressive headache, fever, malaise, lethargy over 1-2 weeks; neck stiffness is often ABSENT due to lack of inflammatory response. Diagnosis: LUMBAR PUNCTURE: Opening pressure is MARKEDLY ELEVATED (> 200-250 mm H2O; cryptococcal capsular polysaccharides block arachnoid villi resorption). CSF: Mild lymphocytic pleocytosis, elevated protein, low glucose. CONFIRMATORY: CRYPTOCOCCAL ANTIGEN (CrAg) lateral flow assay (> 98% sensitive); India ink (capsular halos); fungal culture. THREE PHASES OF THERAPY: 1. INDUCTION THERAPY (at least 2 weeks): LIPOSOMAL AMPHOTERICIN B PLUS INTRAVENOUS FLUCYTOSINE (5-FC). (Fluconazole monotherapy has unacceptably high mortality!). 2. CONSOLIDATION THERAPY (8 weeks): Oral Fluconazole 400 mg daily. 3. MAINTENANCE THERAPY (at least 1 year): Oral Fluconazole 200 mg daily until CD4 > 100 for >= 3 months on ART. MANAGEMENT OF ELEVATED INTRACRANIAL PRESSURE: High ICP is the major cause of death! If opening pressure is >= 250 mm H2O -> PERFORM SERIAL DAILY THERAPEUTIC LUMBAR PUNCTURES to remove CSF until pressure drops to < 200 mm H2O or by 50%. (Mannitol and acetazolamide are ineffective!). DELAY ANTIRETROVIRAL THERAPY (ART) FOR 2 TO 6 WEEKS to prevent fatal immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS)!
necessaryInference: Synthesize cryptococcal meningitis management in advanced HIV: induction therapy with liposomal amphotericin B plus flucytosine, serial therapeutic lumbar punctures for opening pressure >= 250 mm H2O, and delaying ART for 2-6 weeks to avoid fatal IRIS.
strongestDistractor: Oral fluconazole monotherapy combined with immediate initiation of combination antiretroviral therapy within 24 hours of diagnosis
distractorExclusion: Fluconazole monotherapy is inadequate for induction; immediate ART initiation triggers catastrophic central nervous system IRIS; amphotericin B plus flucytosine is mandatory, with ART delayed 2-6 weeks.

references.label: Perfect JR, Dismukes WE, Dromer F, et al. Clinical practice guidelines for the management of cryptococcal disease: 2010 update by the Infectious Diseases Society of America. Clin Infect Dis. 2010;50(3):291-322. PMID: 20047480.

subject: Medicine
topic: Infective Endocarditis Modified Duke Criteria and Surgery Indications
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Infective Endocarditis (IE) Modified Duke Criteria and Surgical Indications: MODIFIED DUKE CRITERIA: Definite IE requires: 2 MAJOR criteria, OR 1 MAJOR + 3 MINOR, OR 5 MINOR criteria. MAJOR CRITERIA: 1. Sustained positive blood cultures for typical organisms (Viridans group streptococci, Streptococcus gallolyticus/bovis, HACEK organisms, Staphylococcus aureus, or Enterococci) from >= 2 separate blood cultures. 2. Endocardial involvement documented by ECHOCARDIOGRAM (transesophageal echocardiogram [TEE] is more sensitive than TTE!): oscillating intracardiac vegetation, abscess, pseudoaneurysm, new dehiscence of prosthetic valve, or NEW VALVULAR REGURGITATION. MINOR CRITERIA: 1. Predisposition (prosthetic valve, prior IE, IV drug use). 2. Fever >= 38.0 C. 3. Vascular phenomena: major arterial emboli, septic pulmonary infarcts, mycotic aneurysm, intracranial hemorrhage, Janeway lesions (painless erythematous macules on palms/soles). 4. Immunologic phenomena: Glomerulonephritis, Osler nodes (PAINFUL violaceous nodules on finger/toe pads), Roth spots (retinal hemorrhages with pale centers), positive Rheumatoid Factor. 5. Microbiological evidence not meeting major criteria. INDICATIONS FOR URGENT CARDIAC SURGERY (VALVE REPLACEMENT): 1. Acute heart failure secondary to severe valvular regurgitation (MOST COMMON INDICATION!). 2. Persistent bacteremia/fever despite 7-10 days of appropriate bactericidal therapy. 3. Fungal endocarditis or multidrug-resistant organisms. 4. Annular/aortic root abscess, fistula, or new conduction block (PR prolongation -> aortic root abscess!). 5. Large mobile vegetation (> 10 mm) with recurrent embolic events.
necessaryInference: Synthesize infective endocarditis Duke criteria and recognize that acute refractory congestive heart failure resulting from severe acute valvular regurgitation is the primary indication for urgent surgical valve replacement.
strongestDistractor: Immediate surgical valve replacement indicated solely for isolated painless Janeway lesions on the palms
distractorExclusion: Janeway lesions are a minor vascular criterion managed with medical antibiotic therapy; surgical valve replacement is indicated for hemodynamic failure, uncontrolled infection, root abscess, or large persistent embolizing vegetations.

references.label: Baddour LM, Wilson WR, Bayer AS, et al. Infective Endocarditis in Adults: Diagnosis, Antimicrobial Therapy, and Management of Complications: A Scientific Statement for Health Professionals From the American Heart Association. Circulation. 2015;132(15):1435-1486. PMID: 26373316.

subject: Medicine
topic: Streptococcus gallolyticus Endocarditis and Mandatory Colonoscopy Screening
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Streptococcus gallolyticus (formerly S. bovis biotype I) bacteremia/endocarditis: Clinical significance: Strong, well-documented association (> 50% to 70%) with OCCULT COLORECTAL ADENOMA OR ADENOCARCINOMA, as well as hepatobiliary pathology. S. gallolyticus thrives in neoplastic colonic mucosa due to altered mucosal barrier and specific adherence factors. GUIDELINE MANDATE: In ANY patient who develops S. gallolyticus bacteremia or endocarditis, a COMPLETE DIAGNOSTIC COLONOSCOPY IS MANDATORY during the hospital stay or shortly after discharge, even if the patient has zero gastrointestinal symptoms, negative fecal occult blood testing, or a normal screening colonoscopy 3 years prior! If colonoscopy is negative, follow-up colonoscopy is recommended within 1 to 2 years.
necessaryInference: Synthesize S. gallolyticus bacteremia/endocarditis as an obligate clinical trigger for complete diagnostic colonoscopy to detect asymptomatic colorectal neoplasia.
strongestDistractor: Discharge with completion of intravenous ceftriaxone without gastrointestinal endoscopy because the patient is entirely asymptomatic
distractorExclusion: Asymptomatic status does not exclude occult colon cancer; S. gallolyticus has an exceptionally strong neoplastic association mandating full colonoscopy.

references.label: Corredoira J, Alonso MP, Coira A, et al. Characteristics of Streptococcus bovis endocarditis and its association with colorectal disease. Medicine (Baltimore). 2012;91(4):208-216. PMID: 22842603.

subject: Medicine
topic: Babesia microti Hemolytic Anemia and Atovaquone Plus Azithromycin Regimen
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Babesiosis (Babesia microti): Vector: Ixodes scapularis tick (co-transmitted with Borrelia burgdorferi and Anaplasma phagocytophilum in the Northeast and upper Midwest US). Pathophysiology: Intraerythrocytic protozoan parasite that invades and lyses red blood cells, causing acute HEMOLYTIC ANEMIA. High-risk severe disease: ASPLENIC PATIENTS (spleen normally clears infected RBCs), elderly, immunocompromised. Clinical: High fevers, drenching sweats, chills, jaundice, dark urine, splenomegaly. Labs: Hemolytic anemia (low Hb, elevated LDH, indirect hyperbilirubinemia, undetectable haptoglobin) and thrombocytopenia. DIAGNOSTIC HALLMARK: Peripheral blood Giemsa/Wright smear showing INTRAERYTHROCYTIC RING FORMS (similar to P. falciparum, but without hemozoin pigment) and classic TETRAD FORMATIONS ("MALTESE CROSS"). FIRST-LINE TREATMENT (mild-to-moderate): ORAL ATOVAQUONE PLUS AZITHROMYCIN for 7-10 days. (Doxycycline treats Lyme and Anaplasma, but has ZERO activity against Babesia!). Severe babesiosis (parasitemia >= 10%, severe hemolysis, pulmonary edema, shock): IV Clindamycin + oral Quinine, plus emergency red blood cell exchange transfusion.
necessaryInference: Recognize Babesia microti as the cause of tick-borne intravascular hemolytic anemia with intraerythrocytic tetrads in a patient failing doxycycline, requiring treatment with atovaquone plus azithromycin.
strongestDistractor: Escalation of intravenous doxycycline dose to 200 mg every 12 hours for refractory Lyme carditis
distractorExclusion: Doxycycline treats bacterial spirochetes (Lyme) and intracellular bacteria (Anaplasma), but is completely inactive against the protozoan parasite Babesia microti.

references.label: Krause PJ, Auwaerter PG, Bannuru RR, et al. Clinical Practice Guidelines by the Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA): 2020 Guideline on Diagnosis and Management of Babesiosis. Clin Infect Dis. 2021;72(2):e49-e64. PMID: 33252615.

subject: Medicine
topic: Anaplasma phagocytophilum vs Ehrlichia chaffeensis Diagnosis and Management
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Anaplasmosis vs Ehrlichiosis: 1. HUMAN GRANULOCYTIC ANAPLASMOSIS (HGA): Caused by Anaplasma phagocytophilum. Vector: IXODES SCAPULARIS tick (Northeast and Upper Midwest US). Target cell: NEUTROPHILS / GRANULOCYTES. Peripheral smear: Intracytoplasmic inclusions (MORULAE) within NEUTROPHILS. 2. HUMAN MONOCYTIC EHRLICHIOSIS (HME): Caused by Ehrlichia chaffeensis. Vector: AMBLYOMMA AMERICANUM (Lone Star tick, Southeast and South Central US). Target cell: MONOCYTES. Peripheral smear: Morulae within MONOCYTES. SHARED CLINICAL AND LAB FEATURES: Acute febrile illness with high fever, headache, myalgias, arthralgias. LAB TRIAD: LEUKOPENIA, THROMBOCYTOPENIA, and ELEVATED TRANSAMINASES (ALT/AST). Rash is rare in anaplasmosis (< 10%), but present in ~30% of ehrlichiosis. TREATMENT OF CHOICE FOR BOTH: DOXYCYCLINE (100 mg PO/IV BID x 10-14 days). Initiate immediately based on clinical suspicion without waiting for PCR or serology!
necessaryInference: Identify Anaplasma phagocytophilum by its tick-borne presentation in the Northeast, the laboratory triad of leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and transaminitis, and intracytoplasmic morulae in neutrophils, requiring immediate doxycycline.
strongestDistractor: Initiation of intravenous vancomycin plus cefepime while withholding tetracyclines pending serologic confirmation
distractorExclusion: Beta-lactams and vancomycin are ineffective against obligate intracellular Anaplasma; delaying doxycycline while awaiting serologies increases morbidity and mortality.

references.label: Biggs HM, Behravesh CB, Bradley KK, et al. Diagnosis and Management of Tickborne Rickettsial Diseases: Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever and Other Spotted Fever Group Rickettsioses, Ehrlichioses, and Anaplasmosis - United States. MMWR Recomm Rep. 2016;65(2):1-44. PMID: 27006448.

subject: Medicine
topic: Clostridioides difficile Infection Severity Stratification and Oral Fidaxomicin
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI) severity stratification and management (IDSA/SHEA guidelines): SEVERITY CRITERIA: 1. INITIAL EPISODE, NON-SEVERE: WBC < 15,000/mm3 AND Serum Creatinine <= 1.5 mg/dL. 2. INITIAL EPISODE, SEVERE: WBC >= 15,000/mm3 OR Serum Creatinine > 1.5 mg/dL. FIRST-LINE REGIMEN (for both non-severe and severe): ORAL FIDAXOMICIN (200 mg BID x 10 days) IS PREFERRED over ORAL VANCOMYCIN (125 mg QID x 10 days) because fidaxomicin (a narrow-spectrum bactericidal macrocyclic RNA polymerase inhibitor) preserves gut microbiome diversity and significantly reduces CDI recurrence rates! (Oral Metronidazole is NO LONGER FIRST-LINE!). 3. FULMINANT CDI: Characterized by HYPOTENSION / SHOCK, ILEUS, or TOXIC MEGACOLON. FULMINANT REGIMEN: HIGH-DOSE ORAL (or via NG tube/rectal enema) VANCOMYCIN (500 mg QID) PLUS INTRAVENOUS METRONIDAZOLE (500 mg TID) PLUS EARLY SURGICAL CONSULTATION for subtotal colectomy or diverting loop ileostomy with colonic vancomycin lavage.
necessaryInference: Stratify C. difficile infection by severity (WBC >= 15k or Cr > 1.5 indicates severe disease) and identify oral fidaxomicin (or oral vancomycin) as the guideline-preferred first-line therapy, distinguishing it from fulminant regimens requiring dual therapy.
strongestDistractor: Oral metronidazole 500 mg three times daily as first-line monotherapy for severe Clostridioides difficile colitis
distractorExclusion: Metronidazole monotherapy is no longer recommended for non-severe or severe CDI due to higher treatment failure rates; oral fidaxomicin or oral vancomycin is first-line.

references.label: Johnson S, Lavergne V, Skinner AM, et al. Clinical Practice Guideline by the Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) and Society for Healthcare Epidemiology of America (SHEA): 2021 Focused Update Guidelines on Management of Clostridioides difficile Infection in Adults. C...

subject: Medicine
topic: Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis Diagnostic Paracentesis and Albumin Infusion
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis (SBP): Clinical presentation: Patient with cirrhotic ascites presenting with fever, chills, abdominal pain, altered mental status (hepatic encephalopathy), or worsening renal failure. DIAGNOSTIC PARACENTESIS MANDATE: Diagnostic abdominal paracentesis must be performed IMMEDIATELY PRIOR TO ANTIBIOTIC THERAPY. DIAGNOSTIC CRITERION: ASCITIC FLUID ABSOLUTE NEUTROPHIL COUNT (ANC) >= 250 cells/mm3 (calculated as: Total ascitic WBC count x % polymorphonuclear cells). Ascitic bacterial culture is typically monomicrobial (E. coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Streptococcus pneumoniae). EMPIRIC ANTIMICROBIAL THERAPY: INTRAVENOUS THIRD-GENERATION CEPHALOSPORIN (CEFTRIAXONE 2 g daily or Cefotaxime 2 g every 8 hours). MANDATORY ADJUNCT TO PREVENT MORTALITY: INTRAVENOUS ALBUMIN INFUSION (1.5 g/kg within 6 hours of diagnosis, and 1.0 g/kg on hospital day 3)! Rationale: Albumin expands effective arterial blood volume, maintains renal perfusion pressure, and significantly reduces the incidence of HEPATORENAL SYNDROME (HRS) and REDUCES INPATIENT MORTALITY from ~30% to < 10% in high-risk patients (BUN > 30 mg/dL, Cr > 1.0 mg/dL, or total bilirubin > 4.0 mg/dL).
necessaryInference: Identify spontaneous bacterial peritonitis by an ascitic fluid absolute neutrophil count >= 250/mm3, and recognize that empiric ceftriaxone must be combined with intravenous albumin to prevent hepatorenal syndrome and reduce mortality.
strongestDistractor: Intravenous ceftriaxone monotherapy while restricting albumin administration to avoid exacerbating portal hypertension
distractorExclusion: Intravenous albumin does not exacerbate portal hypertension; it expands effective intravascular arterial volume, protects renal perfusion, and directly prevents hepatorenal syndrome.

references.label: Runyon BA; AASLD. Introduction to the revised American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases Practice Guideline management of adult patients with ascites due to cirrhosis 2012. Hepatology. 2013;57(4):1651-1653. PMID: 23225437.

subject: Medicine
topic: Neutropenic Fever Empiric Antipseudomonal Monotherapy and Timing
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Febrile Neutropenia (IDSA guidelines): DEFINITIONS: 1. FEVER: Single oral temperature >= 38.3 C (101.0 F) OR sustained temperature >= 38.0 C (100.4 F) over 1 hour. 2. NEUTROPENIA: Absolute Neutrophil Count (ANC) < 500 cells/mm3 OR expected to decrease to < 500 within 48 hours. ANC CALCULATION: ANC = Total WBC x (% segmented neutrophils + % bands). MEDICAL EMERGENCY: Neutropenic patients lack inflammatory signs (no erythema, no purulence, no pulmonary crackles) because there are no neutrophils to recruit! Rapid bacteremia can cause septic shock and death within hours. EMPIRIC MANAGEMENT: 1. OBTAIN 2 SETS OF BLOOD CULTURES (peripheral + central line). 2. INITIATE IMMEDIATE EMPIRIC INTRAVENOUS ANTIPSEUDOMONAL BETA-LACTAM MONOTHERAPY WITHIN 60 MINUTES! Preferred agents: CEFEPIME, MEROPENEM, or PIPERACILLIN-TAZOBACTAM. (Ceftriaxone and ciprofloxacin are inadequate monotherapies!). Vancomycin is NOT routinely indicated upfront unless: hemodynamic shock, catheter-related infection, known MRSA colonization, severe skin/soft tissue infection, or severe mucositis.
necessaryInference: Synthesize febrile neutropenia criteria (ANC < 500 with temp >= 38.3 C) and deduce that immediate antipseudomonal beta-lactam monotherapy (cefepime) within 60 minutes is the mandatory first-line step.
strongestDistractor: Oral levofloxacin outpatient therapy combined with filgrastim (G-CSF) injection and follow-up in 48 hours
distractorExclusion: High-risk febrile neutropenia requires immediate inpatient hospitalization and intravenous antipseudomonal monotherapy; oral fluoroquinolones are strictly for low-risk outpatient candidates.

references.label: Freifeld AG, Bow EJ, Sepkowitz KA, et al. Clinical practice guideline for the use of antimicrobial agents in neutropenic patients with cancer: 2010 update by the Infectious Diseases Society of America. Clin Infect Dis. 2011;52(4):e56-e93. PMID: 21258094.

subject: Surgery
topic: Necrotizing Fasciitis Emergency Debridement and Clindamycin Mechanism
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Necrotizing Fasciitis: Rapidly progressive, life-threatening infection of subcutaneous tissue and deep fascia. TYPES: Type I (Polymicrobial: aerobes + anaerobes; common in diabetics and post-op). Type II (Monomicrobial: Group A Streptococcus [S. pyogenes] +/- S. aureus). CLINICAL HALLMARKS: SEVERE PAIN OUT OF PROPORTION TO PHYSICAL FINDINGS, rapid spread, erythema advancing beyond visible borders, wooden-hard subcutaneous induration, bullae (violaceous/hemorrhagic), skin anesthesia (ischemic necrosis of cutaneous nerves), and crepitus (subcutaneous gas from anaerobic gas-producing bacteria). DEFINITIVE EMERGENCY MANAGEMENT: 1. IMMEDIATE SURGICAL EXPLORATION AND EXTENSIVE OPERATIVE DEBRIDEMENT! (Delaying surgery for imaging or antibiotic response is fatal!). 2. EMPIRIC BROAD-SPECTRUM ANTIBIOTICS: Vancomycin + Piperacillin-tazobactam. 3. MANDATORY ADDITION OF CLINDAMYCIN! WHY CLINDAMYCIN? As a 50S ribosomal subunit inhibitor, clindamycin turns off protein synthesis, HALTING BACTERIAL EXOTOXIN AND SUPERANTIGEN PRODUCTION (SpeA, SpeC) and overcoming the "Eagle effect" (beta-lactams lose bactericidal activity against high bacterial loads in stationary phase).
necessaryInference: Identify necrotizing fasciitis by severe pain out of proportion and rapid progression, recognizing that emergency surgical exploration is the definitive step and that clindamycin is added to inhibit ribosomal exotoxin production.
strongestDistractor: Perform urgent non-contrast lower extremity MRI to confirm fascial fluid collections prior to requesting surgical consultation
distractorExclusion: Obtaining an MRI delays mandatory emergency operative debridement and leads to septic shock and death; surgical exploration is immediately indicated.

references.label: Stevens DL, Bisno AL, Chambers HF, et al. Practice guidelines for the diagnosis and management of skin and soft tissue infections: 2014 update by the Infectious Diseases Society of America. Clin Infect Dis. 2014;59(2):e10-e52. PMID: 24944203.

subject: Medicine
topic: Toxic Shock Syndrome Pathophysiology Superantigen Cytokine Burst
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Toxic Shock Syndrome (TSS): ETIOLOGY: Staphylococcus aureus producing Toxic Shock Syndrome Toxin-1 (TSST-1) or enterotoxins, or Streptococcus pyogenes producing Pyrogenic Exotoxins (SpeA, SpeC). RISK FACTORS: Retained vaginal tampon, nasal packing, surgical wound packing, postpartum infection. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: TSST-1 acts as a SUPERANTIGEN: It binds DIRECTLY and SIMULTANEOUSLY to the invariant region of the MHC CLASS II molecule on antigen-presenting cells AND the V-BETA CHAIN OF THE T-CELL RECEPTOR (TCR), completely bypassing conventional antigen processing! This induces massive, uncontrolled activation of up to 20% of all circulating T cells, triggering a catastrophic "CYTOKINE STORM" with release of massive IL-1, IL-2, TNF-alpha, and IFN-gamma. CLINICAL PRESENTATION: Sudden high fever, profound refractory hypotension (systolic BP < 90 mm Hg), diffuse macular erythroderma resembling sunburn, multiorgan failure (>= 3 systems), and DESQUAMATION OF PALMS AND SOLES 1 to 2 weeks after initial presentation. MANAGEMENT: Immediate source removal (tampon/packing), aggressive IV fluid resuscitation, and IV CLINDAMYCIN (halts toxin synthesis) PLUS IV VANCOMYCIN.
necessaryInference: Synthesize toxic shock syndrome presentation (retained tampon, hypotension, sunburn rash, multiorgan failure) with the superantigen mechanism: direct cross-linking of MHC class II to TCR V-beta chain triggering a massive polyclonal cytokine storm.
strongestDistractor: Complement-mediated classical pathway activation triggered by anti-staphylococcal IgE cross-linking on tissue mast cells
distractorExclusion: TSS is mediated by T-cell superantigen activation and cytokine storm, not mast cell IgE degranulation or classical complement activation.

references.label: Lappin E, Ferguson PE. Gram-positive toxic shock syndromes. Lancet Infect Dis. 2009;9(5):281-290. PMID: 19386408.

subject: Medicine
topic: HIV Opportunistic Infection Prophylaxis CD4 Cutoffs and TMP-SMX Regimens
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate HIV Opportunistic Infection (OI) Prophylaxis: CD4-STRATIFIED THRESHOLDS: 1. CD4 < 200 cells/mm3 (or CD4 percentage < 14%, or oral thrush): PNEUMOCYSTIS JIROVECII PNEUMONIA (PCP). First-line: TRIMETHOPRIM-SULFAMETHOXAZOLE (TMP-SMX) 1 double-strength (DS) tablet daily. Alternatives (if sulfa allergy): Dapsone, Atovaquone, or inhaled Pentamidine. 2. CD4 < 100 cells/mm3 AND POSITIVE TOXOPLASMA IgG SEROLOGY: TOXOPLASMA GONDII ENCEPHALITIS. First-line: TMP-SMX 1 DS daily! (TMP-SMX provides dual cross-protection for both PCP and Toxoplasma!). Alternative: Dapsone + Pyrimethamine + Leucovorin. 3. CD4 < 50 cells/mm3: HISTORICAL MAC PROPHYLAXIS: Historically, oral Azithromycin 1,200 mg weekly was prescribed for Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC). UPDATED IDSA/CDC GUIDELINE UPDATE: PRIMARY MAC PROPHYLAXIS IS NO LONGER ROUTINELY RECOMMENDED IN HIV PATIENTS WITH CD4 < 50 IF THEY ARE INITIATING ANTIRETROVIRAL THERAPY (ART) IMMEDIATELY! ART alone is sufficient to restore mycobacterial immunity without azithromycin toxicity/resistance.
necessaryInference: Identify the precise CD4 threshold and serology indications for opportunistic infection prophylaxis in advanced HIV: initiate TMP-SMX for CD4 < 200 (PCP) and CD4 < 100 with positive Toxoplasma IgG, while withholding routine azithromycin for MAC if initiating immediate ART.
strongestDistractor: Initiate oral azithromycin 1,200 mg weekly for MAC prophylaxis, and defer TMP-SMX until CD4 falls below 50 cells/mm3
distractorExclusion: PCP prophylaxis with TMP-SMX is mandatory when CD4 < 200, and Toxoplasma prophylaxis is indicated at CD4 < 100; azithromycin is no longer recommended if immediate ART is started.

subject: Medicine
topic: Pneumocystis jirovecii Pneumonia Arterial Blood Gas and Steroid Indications
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Pneumocystis jirovecii Pneumonia (PCP) management in HIV: CLINICAL PRESENTATION: Subacute exertional dyspnea, non-productive cough, low-grade fever, hypoxemia out of proportion to exam findings, bilateral diffuse interstitial infiltrates ("ground-glass" opacities), and markedly ELEVATED SERUM LDH (> 250-500 U/L). CRITICAL LIFE-SAVING ADJUNCTIVE THERAPY: MANDATORY ADJUNCTIVE CORTICOSTEROIDS (oral Prednisone or IV Methylprednisolone)! INDICATION THRESHOLDS (ON ROOM-AIR ARTERIAL BLOOD GAS): 1. ARTERIAL PAO2 < 70 MM HG, OR 2. ALVEOLAR-ARTERIAL (A-a) OXYGEN GRADIENT >= 35 MM HG. TIMING: Steroids MUST be administered BEFORE OR CONCURRENTLY WITH the first dose of TMP-SMX! Rationale: Antibiotic-induced fungal lysis releases massive beta-glucan antigens into alveolar spaces, triggering an explosive macrophage inflammatory response that causes severe alveolar-capillary block, acute respiratory deterioration, and death within 48 to 72 hours; steroids prevent this mortality spike.

distractorExclusion: Withholding corticosteroids in severe PCP (PaO2 < 70 or A-a gradient >= 35) increases respiratory failure and mortality from fungal lysis-induced alveolar inflammation.

subject: Obstetrics
topic: Syphilis in Pregnancy Penicillin Allergy and Mandatory Desensitization

ANTIMICROBIAL EFFICACY PRINCIPLE: BENZATHINE PENICILLIN G IS THE ONLY ANTIMICROBIAL REGIMEN DOCUMENTED TO EFFECTIVELY TREAT MATERNAL INFECTION AND CROSS THE PLACENTA TO PREVENT OR TREAT CONGENITAL SYPHILIS IN THE FETUS! ALTERNATIVES (Doxycycline, Tetracycline) ARE STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED IN PREGNANCY due to fetal hepatotoxicity, permanent tooth discoloration, and enamel hypoplasia. Macrolides (Azithromycin) do NOT cross the placenta reliably and have high rates of treponemal resistance. GUIDELINE MANDATE: ANY PREGNANT WOMAN WITH SYPHILIS AND A DOCUMENTED HISTORY OF PENICILLIN ALLERGY MUST UNDERGO SKIN TESTING AND ORAL PENICILLIN DESENSITIZATION IN A MONITORED INPATIENT SETTING, FOLLOWED IMMEDIATELY BY TREATMENT WITH INTRAMUSCULAR BENZATHINE PENICILLIN G! No alternative antibiotic is acceptable.

distractorExclusion: Doxycycline is strictly contraindicated in pregnancy due to fetal teratogenicity (teeth staining, bone growth retardation) and fails to treat the fetus.

subject: Medicine
topic: Jarisch-Herxheimer Reaction Pathophysiology and Clinical Management
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Jarisch-Herxheimer Reaction (JHR): PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Acute, self-limiting systemic inflammatory response occurring within 2 to 24 hours after initiating antimicrobial therapy (most commonly penicillin) for SPIROCHETAL INFECTIONS: Syphilis (Treponema pallidum; seen in up to 50-75% of secondary syphilis), Lyme disease (Borrelia burgdorferi), or Relapsing fever (Borrelia recurrentis). MECHANISM: Rapid antimicrobial-induced killing and lysis of massive numbers of spirochetes releases abundant spirochetal lipoproteins, flagellar proteins, and endotoxin-like pyrogens into the systemic circulation. This triggers an explosive macrophage cytokine burst with massive release of TNF-alpha, IL-6, and IL-8. CLINICAL PRESENTATION: Abrupt onset of shaking rigors, high fevers, diaphoresis, flushing, throbbing headache, tachycardia, myalgias, transient mild hypotension, and VISIBLE EXACERBATION/ERYTHEMA OF PRE-EXISTING SKIN LESIONS (e.g., secondary syphilis macules). CRITICAL MANAGEMENT DISTINCTION: JHR IS A BENIGN, SELF-LIMITING REACTION, NOT AN ALLERGIC DRUG HYPERSENSITIVITY! MANAGEMENT: Reassurance, symptomatic supportive care with oral antipyretics (acetaminophen, ibuprofen), and CONTINUATION OF ANTIMICROBIAL THERAPY (do NOT discontinue penicillin!).
necessaryInference: Distinguish the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction (acute cytokine release from spirochetal lysis 2-24 hours post-penicillin) from true drug allergy, recognizing that management consists of supportive antipyretics and continuation of antibiotics.
strongestDistractor: Immediate administration of intramuscular epinephrine and permanent discontinuation of all penicillin class antibiotics for severe anaphylaxis
distractorExclusion: The reaction is a cytokine surge from bacterial lysis (fever, chills, lesion flare), not IgE-mediated anaphylaxis (no wheezing, stridor, or urticaria); penicillin must be continued.

subject: Medicine
topic: Severe Malaria Artesunate Therapy and G6PD Screening for Primaquine
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Malaria clinical management: SPECIES: Plasmodium falciparum (severe/fatal), P. vivax, P. ovale, P. malariae. SEVERE MALARIA CRITERIA (usually P. falciparum): Parasitemia > 5% to 10%, cerebral malaria (seizures, altered mental status), severe normocytic anemia (Hb < 7), acute kidney injury, pulmonary edema (ARDS), or lactic acidosis (bicarbonate < 15). TREATMENT OF SEVERE MALARIA: INTRAVENOUS ARTESUNATE IS THE FIRST-LINE THERAPY OF CHOICE (superior efficacy and significantly lower mortality compared to intravenous quinidine, with zero risk of cardiac QT prolongation or refractory hypoglycemia!). RADICAL CURE IN P. VIVAX AND P. OVALE: P. vivax and P. ovale form dormant hepatic hypnozoites that cause recurrent relapses months or years later. Treatment requires a blood schizonticide (chloroquine or artemisinin) PLUS PRIMAQUINE or TAFENOQUINE to eradicate liver hypnozoites. CRITICAL SAFETY RULE: GLUCOSE-6-PHOSPHATE DEHYDROGENASE (G6PD) DEFICIENCY TESTING MUST BE PERFORMED PRIOR TO ADMINISTERING PRIMAQUINE! Primaquine induces severe oxidative stress; in G6PD deficiency, failure of glutathione regeneration triggers massive, fatal acute intravascular hemolytic crisis.
necessaryInference: Recognize severe falciparum malaria requiring immediate intravenous artesunate, and synthesize that eradication of dormant hypnozoites in non-falciparum strains requires primaquine with mandatory prior G6PD screening to prevent acute hemolysis.
strongestDistractor: Initiate oral chloroquine monotherapy combined with immediate high-dose primaquine without checking enzyme levels
distractorExclusion: Severe malaria requires intravenous artesunate, not oral chloroquine; administering primaquine without G6PD testing can trigger catastrophic hemolytic crisis.

references.label: CDC. Treatment of Malaria: Guidelines for Clinicians (United States). Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. 2021. PMID: 34914669.

subject: Surgery
topic: Diabetic Foot Osteomyelitis Diagnosis Probe-to-Bone and Bone Biopsy
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Diabetic Foot Osteomyelitis: EVALUATION IN NON-HEALING ULCER: Neuropathy + peripheral artery disease -> painless foot ulcer. SUSPICION FOR OSTEOMYELITIS: Ulcer area > 2 cm2, duration > 1-2 weeks, depth to tendon or bone, or elevated ESR (> 70 mm/hr). BEDSIDE TEST: PROBE-TO-BONE TEST: A sterile, blunt metallic probe is inserted into the ulcer; feeling a hard, gritty, bone-like surface has a POSITIVE PREDICTIVE VALUE > 85-90% for underlying osteomyelitis! IMAGING: Initial: Plain radiographs (X-rays). Caveat: X-rays can be FALSELY NORMAL for the first 10-14 days (cortical erosion and periosteal reaction require 30-50% bone mineral loss). DEFINITIVE IMAGING OF CHOICE: MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING (MRI) OF THE FOOT (highest sensitivity and specificity for cortical destruction and bone marrow edema). MICROBIOLOGICAL GOLD STANDARD: BONE BIOPSY WITH CULTURE AND HISTOPATHOLOGY! SUPERFICIAL WOUND SWABS OF THE ULCER BASE ARE CONTRAINDICATED TO GUIDE ANTIBIOTICS (they culture colonizing superficial skin flora rather than true deep osseous pathogens!).
necessaryInference: Recognize that deep non-healing diabetic foot ulcers with positive probe-to-bone test require MRI for anatomical evaluation and definitive bone biopsy for microbiological culture, while superficial swabs are unreliable.
strongestDistractor: Swab the superficial ulcer base for aerobic and anaerobic bacterial cultures to guide oral antibiotic therapy
distractorExclusion: Superficial swabs reflect colonizing skin flora, not true osseous pathogens; definitive microbiological diagnosis requires deep bone biopsy and culture.

subject: Medicine
topic: Catheter-Associated Urinary Tract Infection Management and Catheter Exchange
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Catheter-Associated Urinary Tract Infection (CAUTI; IDSA guidelines): DEFINITION: Symptomatic UTI in a patient with an indwelling urinary catheter (or removed within 48 h): fever, rigors, altered mental status, flank pain, or suprapubic pain with bacteriuria (>= 10^3 CFU/mL) and pyuria. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Indwelling catheters in place for >= 1-2 weeks develop dense, resilient MICROBIAL BIOFILMS on both internal and external catheter surfaces. Biofilm bacteria are embedded in an extracellular polysaccharide matrix, highly resistant to systemic antibiotics, and represent colonizing organisms rather than true active bladder infection. GUIDELINE MANAGEMENT MANDATE: 1. ASSESS CONTINUED NEED: If the catheter is no longer clinically indicated, REMOVE IT IMMEDIATELY! 2. IF THE CATHETER HAS BEEN IN PLACE FOR >= 2 WEEKS AND STILL CANNOT BE SAFELY DISCONTINUED: REMOVE AND REPLACE THE INDWELLING FOLEY CATHETER PRIOR TO COLLECTING THE URINE CULTURE SPECIMEN! 3. Collect the urine culture from the FRESHLY PLACED catheter (or midstream clean-catch after removal). Culturing urine through an old, biofilm-colonized catheter port leads to false microbiological results, targeting colonizers rather than true bladder pathogens.
necessaryInference: Identify that an indwelling Foley catheter in place for >= 2 weeks in a patient with suspected CAUTI must be removed and replaced prior to obtaining a diagnostic urine culture to avoid sampling colonizing biofilm flora.
strongestDistractor: Aspirate urine immediately from the sampling port of the existing 3-week-old indwelling catheter to ensure rapid microbiological identification
distractorExclusion: Culturing urine from a catheter in place > 2 weeks samples colonizing intraluminal biofilms; replacing the catheter prior to urine sampling is mandatory.

subject: Medicine
topic: Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia Empiric Regimen and Dual Antipseudomonal Rule
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia (VAP; IDSA/ATS guidelines): DEFINITION: Hospital-acquired pneumonia developing >= 48 hours AFTER ENDOTRACHEAL INTUBATION. DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA: New or progressive pulmonary infiltrate on chest radiography PLUS >= 2 of: fever (> 38 C), purulent endotracheal secretions, leukocytosis or leukopenia, and worsening oxygenation (declining PaO2/FiO2 ratio). RISK FACTORS FOR MULTIDRUG-RESISTANT (MDR) PATHOGENS: Prior IV antibiotic use within 90 days, septic shock at VAP onset, ARDS preceding VAP, >= 5 days of hospitalization, or local ICU MRSA prevalence > 10-20%. EMPIRIC ANTIMICROBIAL REGIMEN IN HIGH-RISK VAP: MANDATES A THREE-DRUG COMBINATION: 1. ONE AGENT AGAINST MRSA: Vancomycin (trough 15-20 mcg/mL) OR Linezolid. PLUS 2. TWO AGENTS ACTIVE AGAINST PSEUDOMONAS AERUGINOSA FROM DIFFERENT PHARMACOLOGICAL CLASSES! Dual antipseudomonal options: An antipseudomonal beta-lactam (Cefepime, Piperacillin-tazobactam, or Meropenem) PLUS an antipseudomonal fluoroquinolone (Ciprofloxacin or Levofloxacin) OR an aminoglycoside (Amikacin, Tobramycin). Monotherapy or single gram-negative coverage is inadequate in high-risk VAP!
necessaryInference: Synthesize ventilator-associated pneumonia with multidrug-resistance risk factors (intubated >= 48 hours, prior antibiotics) and deduce the guideline mandate for empiric MRSA coverage plus two antipseudomonal agents from different classes.
strongestDistractor: Intravenous ceftriaxone plus azithromycin to provide standard empiric community-acquired pneumonia coverage
distractorExclusion: Ceftriaxone and azithromycin have zero activity against MRSA or Pseudomonas aeruginosa, which cause the vast majority of ventilator-associated pneumonias.

subject: Obstetrics
topic: Acute Pyelonephritis in Pregnancy Inpatient Admission and Parenteral Cephalosporins
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Acute Pyelonephritis in Pregnancy: PHYSIOLOGY: High gestational progesterone causes smooth muscle relaxation and ureteral hypomotility/dilation (hydroureter); enlarging uterus causes mechanical ureteral compression (predominantly RIGHT-SIDED due to dextrorotation of uterus). SEVERE COMPLICATIONS: Pyelonephritis in pregnancy carries high maternal-fetal morbidity: maternal septic shock, ACUTE RESPIRATORY DISTRESS SYNDROME (ARDS; endotoxin-induced alveolar capillary damage), preterm labor, and low birth weight. MANAGEMENT MANDATE: ALL PREGNANT PATIENTS WITH PYELONEPHRITIS REQUIRE IMMEDIATE HOSPITAL ADMISSION FOR PARENTERAL (INTRAVENOUS) BETA-LACTAM ANTIBIOTICS! First-line empiric regimens: INTRAVENOUS CEFTRIAXONE, Ampicillin-sulbactam, or Cefepime. CONTRAINDICATED AGENTS: Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin) are strictly contraindicated (fetal cartilage and joint damage); TMP-SMX is contraindicated in the 1st trimester (neural tube defects) and near term (kernicterus). Continue IV therapy until afebrile for 24-48 hours, switch to oral antibiotics for 10-14 days total, followed by low-dose daily suppressive therapy until delivery.

distractorExclusion: Fluoroquinolones are strictly contraindicated in pregnancy due to fetal chondrotoxicity, and pyelonephritis in pregnancy mandates inpatient intravenous admission.

subject: Obstetrics
topic: Asymptomatic Bacteriuria in Pregnancy Screening and Antimicrobial Regimens
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Asymptomatic Bacteriuria in Pregnancy: DEFINITION: Presence of >= 10^5 CFU/mL of a single pathogen on clean-catch urine specimen in a patient WITHOUT any symptoms of urinary tract infection (no dysuria, urgency, or frequency). SCREENING MANDATE: Routine screening with clean-catch urine culture is performed for ALL PREGNANT WOMEN AT 12 TO 16 WEEKS GESTATION (or initial prenatal visit). CLINICAL CONTRAST: In NON-PREGNANT adults, asymptomatic bacteriuria is benign and treatment is CONTRAINDICATED (increases antibiotic resistance without clinical benefit). IN PREGNANCY, ASYMPTOMATIC BACTERIURIA MUST ALWAYS BE TREATED! SAFE FIRST-LINE ORAL REGIMENS: Oral Cephalexin, Amoxicillin-clavulanate, Nitrofurantoin (avoid near delivery/term due to neonatal hemolytic anemia), or single-dose Fosfomycin. MANDATORY FOLLOW-UP: A repeat urine culture (TEST-OF-CURE) MUST BE OBTAINED 1 TO 2 WEEKS AFTER TREATMENT COMPLETION to verify bacterial eradication!

subject: Medicine
topic: Sexually Transmitted Cervicitis and Urethritis Updated CDC Therapy Guidelines

DIAGNOSTIC TEST OF CHOICE: NUCLEIC ACID AMPLIFICATION TESTING (NAAT) from first-catch urine (men) or vaginal/endocervical swab (women). UPDATED GUIDELINE THERAPY (REPLACED HISTORICAL REGIMENS): 1. FOR GONOCOCCAL INFECTION (or empiric coverage when gonorrhea is not excluded): CEFTRIAXONE 500 MG INTRAMUSCULARLY (IM) AS A SINGLE DOSE (increased from historical 250 mg due to rising MICs; 1,000 mg IM if weight >= 150 kg). 2. FOR CHLAMYDIA TRACHOMATIS: ORAL DOXYCYCLINE 100 MG TWICE DAILY FOR 7 DAYS IS FIRST-LINE! Why not Azithromycin 1 g single dose? Extensive randomized trials demonstrate that azithromycin has inferior cure rates for rectal chlamydia and has driven massive macrolide resistance in Mycoplasma genitalium and Gonorrhea! topic: Pelvic Inflammatory Disease Outpatient vs Inpatient Regimens and Anaerobe Coverage

Surgical emergencies cannot be excluded (e.g., acute appendicitis). 4. Severe illness, high fever (> 38.5 C), nausea, vomiting, or peritonitis. 5. subject: Medicine
topic: Myxedema Coma Resuscitation and Hydrocortisone Preceding Levothyroxine

If the patient has underlying secondary hypothyroidism or concomitant autoimmune primary adrenal insufficiency (polyglandular autoimmune syndrome), administering thyroid hormone without glucocorticoids precipitates catastrophic, fatal acute adrenal crisis!

subject: Medicine
topic: Thyroid Storm Multimodal Medical Therapy and Potassium Iodide Timing
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Thyroid Storm management: Medical emergency with mortality > 20%. Burch-Wartofsky Point Scale >= 45: Severe hyperpyrexia (temp > 39-40 C), extreme tachycardia/atrial fibrillation, agitation/delirium/psychosis, nausea/vomiting/jaundice, and high-output heart failure. FOUR-TIER MULTIMODAL THERAPY: 1. BETA-BLOCKER: Propranolol (blocks beta-adrenergic receptors and inhibits peripheral 5'-monodeiodinase T4-to-T3 conversion) or IV esmolol. 2. THIONAMIDE: PROPYLTHIOURACIL (PTU) preferred over methimazole in acute storm (PTU blocks both new thyroid hormone synthesis via thyroid peroxidase AND blocks peripheral conversion of T4 to T3). 3. INORGANIC IODINE (Lugol solution or Saturated Solution of Potassium Iodide [SSKI]): Inhibits thyroid hormone release via the WOLFF-CHAIKOFF EFFECT. CRITICAL TIMING RULE: IODINE MUST BE ADMINISTERED AT LEAST 1 HOUR AFTER THIONAMIDE! Why? If iodine is given before thionamide, the thyroid gland utilizes the exogenous iodine as a substrate to synthesize and release massive new waves of thyroid hormone (Jod-Basedow phenomenon), worsening the storm! 4. INTRAVENOUS GLUCOCORTICOIDS (Hydrocortisone): Further reduces T4-to-T3 conversion and treats relative adrenal exhaustion.

distractorExclusion: Administering iodine before thionamides provides iodine substrate that the unblocked thyroid peroxidase incorporates into thyroid hormone, worsening storm.

subject: Medicine
topic: Diabetic Ketoacidosis Potassium Repletion and Insulin Timing Thresholds
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA) management (ADA Guidelines): DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA: Blood glucose > 250 mg/dL, arterial pH < 7.30, serum bicarbonate < 18 mEq/L, and elevated anion gap (> 12) with positive serum/urine ketones. CRITICAL MANAGEMENT PILLARS: 1. FLUID RESUSCITATION: 0.9% Normal Saline (1-1.5 L/hr initially) to restore intravascular volume. 2. POTASSIUM MANAGEMENT — THE ABSOLUTE SAFETY THRESHOLDS: Total body potassium is ALWAYS depleted in DKA (due to osmotic diuresis and urinary loss), even if initial serum K is normal or elevated! Insulin drives potassium intracellularly. IF SERUM POTASSIUM IS < 3.3 mEq/L: WITHHOLD INSULIN IMMEDIATELY! Administer aggressive IV potassium chloride (20-40 mEq/hr) until serum K > 3.3 mEq/L! Giving insulin when K < 3.3 mEq/L causes fatal hypokalemia, cardiac arrest, and respiratory muscle paralysis! If K is 3.3 to 5.3 mEq/L: Give 20-30 mEq K per liter of IV fluid alongside insulin. If K > 5.3 mEq/L: Start insulin, check K every 2 hours. 3. DEXTROSE ADDITION: When serum glucose drops to <= 200 mg/dL, ADD 5% DEXTROSE TO IV FLUIDS while continuing insulin infusion until the ANION GAP CLOSES (anion gap <= 12 and bicarbonate >= 18 mEq/L)!

subject: Medicine
topic: Primary Adrenal Insufficiency Cosyntropin Stimulation and Crisis Management
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Primary vs Secondary Adrenal Insufficiency: PRIMARY ADRENAL INSUFFICIENCY (Addison Disease): Autoimmune adrenalitis (most common in US), TB (worldwide), or bilateral adrenal hemorrhage (Waterhouse-Friderichsen). Mineralocorticoid deficiency (aldosterone): HYPONATREMIA, HYPERKALEMIA, and NON-ANION GAP METABOLIC ACIDOSIS (aldosterone normally secretes K+ and H+ in exchange for Na+). 3. Adrenal androgen deficiency: loss of pubic/axillary hair in women. 4. HIGH ACTH / POMC: ACTH hypersecretion stimulates melanocortin-1 receptors, causing generalized HYPERPIGMENTATION (palmar creases, buccal mucosa, scars). SECONDARY ADRENAL INSUFFICIENCY (Pituitary ACTH deficiency): Aldosterone is PRESERVED (regulated by renin-angiotensin system, not ACTH!); therefore, NO HYPERKALEMIA and NO HYPERPIGMENTATION! DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP: High-dose COSYNTROPIN (synthetic ACTH) stimulation test: measure cortisol at 0, 30, and 60 minutes; FAILURE OF CORTISOL TO RISE > 18 mcg/dL confirms adrenal insufficiency. distractorExclusion: Hyperpigmentation with hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, and hypotension indicates adrenal failure (Addison disease), not hypercortisolism (Cushing disease).

topic: Pheochromocytoma Preoperative Alpha-Blockade Mandate Before Beta-Blockers

FIRST-LINE: IRREVERSIBLE NON-COMPETITIVE ALPHA-ADRENERGIC BLOCKADE (PHENOXYBENZAMINE, or selective alpha-1 blockers like doxazosin/terazosin) INITIATED 10 TO 14 DAYS PRIOR TO SURGERY. 2. SECOND-LINE (AFTER ADEQUATE ALPHA-BLOCKADE): BETA-ADRENERGIC BLOCKADE (e.g., Propranolol, Atenolol) ADDED 2 TO 3 DAYS PRE-OP TO CONTROL TACHYCARDIA. THE DEADLY CLINICAL CONTRAINDICATION: BETA-BLOCKERS MUST NEVER BE INITIATED BEFORE ALPHA-BLOCKERS! Why? Beta-2 receptors mediate peripheral vasodilation. Blocking beta-2 receptors while leaving alpha-1 receptors unblocked results in UNOPPOSED ALPHA-1 ADRENERGIC STIMULATION, causing catastrophic malignant hypertensive crisis, severe coronary vasospasm, myocardial infarction, and fatal acute pulmonary edema!

subject: Medicine
topic: Primary Hyperaldosteronism Screening Aldosterone-Renin Ratio and Sampling
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Primary Hyperaldosteronism (Conn Syndrome): ETIOLOGIES: 1. Unilateral aldosterone-producing adenoma (APA; ~35-40%). 2. Bilateral idiopathic adrenal hyperplasia (IAH; ~60%). CLINICAL: Hypertension refractory to >= 3 drugs, unprovoked hypokalemia (or severe diuretic-induced hypokalemia), metabolic alkalosis, mild hypernatremia (no overt edema due to 'aldosterone escape'!). SCREENING TEST OF CHOICE: PLASMA ALDOSTERONE CONCENTRATION TO PLASMA RENIN ACTIVITY (PAC/PRA) RATIO: PAC/PRA > 20 WITH PAC > 15 ng/dL is positive. CONFIRMATORY TESTING: Oral sodium loading test or IV saline infusion test (failure of aldosterone to suppress < 5-10 ng/dL confirms autonomous production). SUBTYPE LOCALIZATION MANDATE: ADRENAL CT is performed first. HOWEVER, ADRENAL VEIN SAMPLING (AVS) IS MANDATORY PRIOR TO SURGERY IN PATIENTS > 35 YEARS OLD TO DISTINGUISH UNILATERAL ADENOMA FROM BILATERAL HYPERPLASIA! (CT can show non-functioning incidentalomas in elderly patients!). TREATMENT: Unilateral adenoma -> Laparoscopic adrenalectomy. Bilateral hyperplasia -> Medical therapy with Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists (SPIRONOLACTONE or EPLERENONE).

distractorExclusion: Adrenal incidentalomas are common in adults > 35; proceeding to surgery without adrenal vein sampling risks removing an inactive nodule and leaving bilateral hyperplasia untreated.

subject: Medicine
topic: Cushing Syndrome Stepwise Diagnostic Algorithm and High-Dose Dexamethasone
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Cushing Syndrome diagnostic algorithm: STEP 1: ESTABLISH HYPERCORTISOLEMIA (requires >= 2 concordant first-line tests): 1. 24-hour urinary free cortisol (UFC; > 3-4x normal), 2. Late-night salivary cortisol (elevated due to loss of normal diurnal nadir), 3. Overnight low-dose (1-mg) Dexamethasone Suppression Test (DST; serum cortisol >= 1.8 mcg/dL at 8 AM confirms failure to suppress). STEP 2: MEASURE PLASMA ACTH: ACTH < 5 pg/mL = ACTH-INDEPENDENT (adrenal adenoma/carcinoma -> perform Adrenal CT). ACTH >= 15-20 pg/mL = ACTH-DEPENDENT (Cushing disease vs Ectopic ACTH). STEP 3: DIFFERENTIATE CUSHING DISEASE (pituitary ACTH adenoma) FROM ECTOPIC ACTH (small cell lung cancer, bronchial carcinoid): HIGH-DOSE (8-MG) DEXAMETHASONE SUPPRESSION TEST: Pituitary corticotroph adenomas retain partial negative feedback, SUPPRESSING CORTISOL BY > 50%! Ectopic ACTH tumors DO NOT SUPPRESS (< 50% suppression). CRH Stimulation Test: Pituitary adenomas show robust rise in ACTH/cortisol; ectopic tumors do not respond. GOLD STANDARD FOR LOCALIZATION: INFERIOR PETROSAL SINUS SAMPLING (IPSS) confirms pituitary source (central-to-peripheral ACTH gradient > 2:1 baseline, > 3:1 after CRH).

distractorExclusion: Hypercortisolemia must first be confirmed with >= 2 first-line tests, followed by ACTH measurement and high-dose dexamethasone testing, before neurosurgical intervention.

subject: Medicine
topic: SIADH vs Cerebral Salt Wasting Volume Status and Treatment Divergence
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate SIADH vs Cerebral Salt Wasting (CSW) in neurosurgical/CNS patients: Both present with hyponatremia and high urine sodium (> 40 mEq/L). SYNDROME OF INAPPROPRIATE ANTIDIURETIC HORMONE (SIADH): Clinically EUVOLEMIC (normal skin turgor, moist membranes, flat JVP, no orthostasis, no edema). Labs: Serum Osm < 275 mOsm/kg, Urine Osm > 100-300 mOsm/kg, Urine Na > 30-40 mEq/L, LOW BUN and URIC ACID (due to dilution and reduced proximal reabsorption). FIRST-LINE TREATMENT: FLUID RESTRICTION (500-1000 mL/day), oral salt tablets, or vasopressin receptor antagonists (vaptans). 2. CEREBRAL SALT WASTING (CSW): Clinically HYPOVOLEMIC (dry mucous membranes, decreased skin turgor, tachycardia, orthostatic hypotension, flat neck veins, negative cumulative fluid balance). Pathophysiology: Excessive release of BNP/ANP or impaired renal sympathetic tone causes massive urinary sodium and water wasting. Labs: High urine Na (> 40-100), ELEVATED BUN/CREATININE RATIO (prerenal azotemia), high hematocrit. FIRST-LINE TREATMENT: INTRAVENOUS ISOTONIC (0.9%) SALINE VOLUME RESUSCITATION! THE FATAL ERROR: FLUID RESTRICTION IN CSW CAUSES SEVERE HYPOVOLEMIC SHOCK, CEREBRAL VASOSPASM, AND FATAL ISCHEMIC BRAIN INFARCTION!

distractorExclusion: Fluid restriction in a hypovolemic patient with cerebral salt wasting precipitates severe hypotension, cerebral vasospasm, and stroke.
